editorials.title: Unkind cuts: On the Telangana and Karnataka electoral rolls
editorials.passage:
The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process being conducted by the Election Commission of India (ECI) is increasingly leading to a clear case of disenfranchisement in several parts of India. Marauding on after a judgment by the Supreme Court of India allowed it to proceed, the SIR has now struck out a fifth of the names from the electoral rolls in Telangana and Karnataka — nearly 22% and 19.5% respectively — and among the highest in the country. The cuts are steepest in their capital cities — five constituencies in Bengaluru have lost more than half of their electors while nine of Hyderabad’s 15 have seen deletions of more than 40% . Cuts of this kind cannot simply be a trimming of bloated rolls at the margins. If they are accurate, the ECI’s own summary revision processes were yielding bloated rolls in recent elections, and doing so in the very places with high net in-migration from the rest of India. And if the deletions are to be justified, those struck off the rolls must have left the States — a move within Karnataka or Telangana would only relocate a voter’s name on the same State roll, not remove it altogether. Yet, this is neither borne out by recent survey data nor by the government’s own population estimates.

During the Bihar SIR, the Court asked why political parties had filed so few objections, seeking inclusion of wrongly deleted names; that question might hold true for the Southern States as well. A plausible reason could be that the voter id is useful to a citizen only once in a few years, leading to less alacrity on their part. This may explain why a process that puts the onus on electors yields cuts of this scale. Meanwhile, proving a smoking gun in the data is difficult because of the ECI’s opacity. It has not published the elector-to-population ratio for any State so far during the revision even though doing so is mandatory and is the only test of under-enrolment. The Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer has not even bothered to release a gender-wise breakdown of the deletions, instead scattering the lists across several Google Drive links without the old booth numbers, making verification arduous. The outcome of such shoddiness is visible in West Bengal, where the ECI’s dubious “logical discrepancy” process disenfranchised lakhs of electors, forcing them to seek redress before tribunals set up under the aegis of the Court. Months after the elections, records obtained under a Right to Information request show that barely 82,000 of the nearly 38 lakh appeals before the 19 tribunals have been decided, with more than 90% of those decisions favouring electors seeking restoration. The ECI — an institution once envied even by wealthier democracies for bringing large numbers of Indians to the polling booth — is now an obstacle to universal adult franchise.

editorials.title: Deferred rivalry: On the U.S. Open
editorials.passage:
The Carlos Alcaraz-Jannik Sinner rivalry is no doubt this era’s defining matchup, but it has also been punctuated by long pauses. In early 2025, Sinner was absent for three months as he served a doping-related ban; this season, Alcaraz was out of action for four months from mid-April owing to a troublesome wrist. Just when it seemed that the two leading lights will come face to face at the US Open starting Sunday, Sinner has been waylaid by a knee injury. In 2025, they met six times in six months; there has just been a solitary duel in the subsequent nine. In a way, the postponement of the battle may suit Alcaraz, for the seven-time Major champion has not played a competitive singles fixture since Barcelona in April. The Spaniard has warmed up for Flushing Meadows with two mixed doubles matches partnering the legendary Serena Williams, but a best-of-five-sets contest is a significant step-up. The 23-year-old will open against Roman Safiullin — a tricky player who beat Alcaraz in 2023 on a Paris hard-court and reached the Wimbledon fourth round this year — and is drawn to meet the in-form American Ben Shelton in the quarterfinal. Potential semifinal opponents include 24-time Slam titlist Novak Djokovic and 2021 US Open winner Daniil Medvedev, which makes the defending champion’s path challenging.

However, Djokovic and Medvedev are on their own tough journeys. The 39-year-old Serb is no longer the once-renowned hard-court master, and lost his lone match – in Cincinnati – after the semifinal reverse to Sinner at Wimbledon. Medvedev was last in a Major final at the 2024 Australian Open and is without a trophy since February. Alexander Zverev thus has a golden opportunity to make his big breakthrough on his favourite surface. Without Sinner, the German will be the top seed, and following the French Open triumph and Wimbledon runner-up finish, the 29-year-old will be confidence personified. Among women, two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka would have liked to be that player, but the Belarusian World No. 1 has wobbled of late and seen her lead at the top cut to less than 450 points. Her chief challenger Elena Rybakina may be racing against time to recover from an ankle injury, but with Iga Swiatek, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula all in impressive form leading into New York, Sabalenka will have a daunting task. Wimbledon winner Linda Noskova will be looking for a worthy follow-up while the fast-rising 21-year-old from the Philippines, Alexandra Eala, will hope to continue her recent eye-popping run. With Serena and Venus Williams set to pair up in doubles, there will be a rich sprinkling of stardust too.

editorials.title: Treat Himalayas as one disaster zone, coordinate data to improve response
editorials.passage: Wednesday's furious flash floods and landslides on the Nepal-Tibet border show how closely interconnected the Himalayan region is as an ecological disaster zone. An extreme event in the mountains can affect communities far away, across national borders. What happens in one part of the Himalayas cannot be regarded as any one country’s problem. The danger extends across the region.For India, the concern is immediate and geographical. The Tibetan-origin Lhende river, where the flooding initiated, forms the Bhote Koshi in Nepal, which flows downstream as the Trishuli and the Narayani, which flows farther into India as the Gandak. What happens in the upper reaches of the river system can affect people downstream. The Himalayan rivers make cooperation on disasters a practical necessity, whatever the political circumstances.The latest floods also point to a changing pattern of Himalayan risk. No rain fell when flooding occurred. The trigger appears to have been a glacier collapse and an ice-rock avalanche, followed by a temporary blockage and the sudden release of water and debris. This differs from the familiar picture of flooding and shows why disaster warnings in the mountains have to look beyond rainfall.Weather forecasts will need to be backed by closer monitoring of glaciers, unstable slopes and other sources of sudden flooding. In the mountains, such events can develop rapidly, leaving little time to evacuate. Climate change must be part of this discussion, with continuously evaluated evidence. The broader changes in the Himalayas are clear. The region is warming and its glaciers are rapidly losing ice. These changes make it important to understand how risks are evolving rather than assume that past patterns will always hold..Infrastructure presents another challenge. Roads, bridges, hydropower and tourism facilities are necessary for Himalayan communities and their economies. But projects in the mountains must account carefully for unstable slopes, glacial lakes, changing river flows and the risk of sudden landslides and floods.India can play an important role in strengthening cooperation with Nepal and, where possible, China. A Himalayan disaster compact could provide for sharing satellite and river data, joint monitoring of vulnerable areas, better early-warning systems and closer coordination during rescue and evacuation. editorials.title: Hijab-clad girls puncture patriarchy in Onam dance
editorials.passage: A video clip of hijab-clad students celebrating Onam in a high school in Kerala’s Malappuram district, where Muslims make up more than two-thirds of the population, has drawn widespread appreciation online. Wearing traditional Kasavu-themed attires along with matching hijabs, these girls were recorded dancing with their schoolmates during celebrations held at their institutions. The video stood out among the thousands of similar ones that flooded social media over the past few days by showing that religion was no bar when it came to embracing the festival’s inclusive spirit with zest. The dance acquired added significance because these young Muslim girls were braving the diktats of orthodox religious scholars who had warned against partaking in the festivities. Such fatwas were issued during the past few Onams, too. But a number of young Muslim girls defied them this time to dance along unapologetically. Some girls even posted on social media asking the clerics to explain the rationale behind banning them from participating in Onam.It is indeed curious that the clerics who were offended by girls’ participation in the festivities were silent on Muslim boys taking part. It exposes the fact that religion is not the real issue here, but the patriarchy of clergymen who could not digest the fact that girls were no longer confined within the circle they had drawn. Such diktats, when openly defied, only serve to weaken their standing within the community even as they try to accentuate divisive feelings during a joyous occasion. Sensible voices within the community should restrain the clerics from making remarks that leave a negative imprint on society as a whole. It was a harmonious gesture of Panakkad Sayyid Sadik Ali Shihab Thangal, state president of Indian Union Muslim League and one of the most respected figures among Muslims in Kerala, to take part in the celebrations..As these young girls wearing traditional costumes danced their way to glory, the secular psyche of Kerala clapped in approval. Women from all communities keep breaking glass ceilings and finding their own space in all walks of life. They should not be restrained with patriarchal decrees that intend to curb their freedom. As these young girls showed, perhaps the best way to smash patriarchy is to dance on it..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | A jeweller's eye
editorials.passage: Ebrahim Alkazi, who expanded the vocabulary and visuals of theatre, also had a keen eye for images old and new. His vision for preserving the old can be seen in his carefully-maintained archive of some of the earliest photographs of India, now curated by his grandson Rahaab Allana. Along with his wife Roshen, Alkazi also supported modernist women artists. Among them was Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese pop art pioneer who did to polka dots what Pablo Neruda saw spring doing to the cherry trees. The Center for International Contemporary Arts, which Alkazi founded in New York, revived Kusama’s career in 1989 with a solo show that thrust her unapologetic art and self into the global imagination. Her recent passing reminds us that, in the world of art, it takes one to know one..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Rethinking Progress
editorials.passage:
On the morning of August 26, a wall of water and rock roared down the Bhotekashi valley where Nepal meets Tibet, a glacier somewhere high above the clouds having broken loose and turned an ordinary river into an instrument of annihilation. Villages disappeared within minutes, hydropower stations that had taken years to build were flattened, and a bridge that had carried traders and pilgrims across that border for generations was gone before anyone downstream even understood what was happening. 

Rescue teams in Rasuwa were still wading through mud in search of the missing when television screens began carrying near identical images from across the frontier in China, where weeks of saturated soil in Guangxi had turned routine monsoon rain into landslides, where tornadoes tore through Hubei, and where the thermometers in Xinjiang touched fifty degrees Celsius in June. Two neighbouring nations, one catastrophe repeating itself in different ways, and a planet serving notice in the plainest language it has that something in the way we have organised our relationship with it has failed. 

It would be a mistake to see Rasuwa and Guangxi as unrelated and separate tragedies, acts of nature to be mourned and then forgotten till the next tragedy. They are data points in a pattern the Sustainable Development Goals were meant to interrupt and did not. The report on those Goals, drawn up as 2030 approaches, brings out some uncomfortable truths. Barely a third of the targets are on track, close to half are crawling forward too slowly to matter, and a worrying number have actually reversed since 2015. 

What Rasuwa adds to that report is not a new statistic but a human face for it, the particular horror of a glacier that has held firm for millennia choosing this decade to let go, of a warning system built with real ingenuity and genuine cooperation between two governments being simply outrun by the speed of the collapse it was designed to detect. When the very early warning infrastructure fails because the disaster moves faster than any siren, the perspective should not be that the warning systems need upgrading. It is that the condition producing the disaster needs addressing. 

This is the deeper failure of the last three decades of climate governance, that so much of it has been remediation dressed up as strategy. We rebuild the bridge, relocate the village, strengthen the reservoir bunds, deploy the radar, expand the sponge city, and each of these is needed and none of them is sufficient, because every one of them treats the flood as the problem rather than as the symptom. 

The permafrost that once held the Himalaya together is thinning because the planet is warming, and the planet is warming because the global economic model built on extraction and consumerism has spent two centuries treating the earth as a quarry rather than as a living system within its own thresholds. A country can install every early warning system science can devise and still be surprised, because the mitigation plans are built on a paradigm that only asks how much damage can be prevented and never asks what kind of relationship with the earth would prevent the damage from arising in the first place. 

That distinction, between preventing harm and addressing its root, is where the conversation must now move, and it is here that regenerative development offers something sustainability never could. Sustainability, honestly examined, is a defensive posture, asking us to consume a little more carefully and pollute a little more slowly so that the next generation inherits a world no more ruined than the one we received. 

Regeneration asks an entirely different question, not how much can be taken before something breaks but how much can be given back so that a watershed, a forest, a community, a civilisation, becomes more capable of holding itself together than it was before. A regenerative approach to the Himalayas would not stop at monitoring glaciers. It would ask what combination of afforestation, community stewardship of upper catchments, and restrain in how those fragile slopes are built upon might restore the resilience that industrial development has spent decades eroding. 

It would treat the mountain not as a hazard to be managed but as living ecosystem whose vitality is our responsibility to renew. India carries civilisational resources for exactly this reframing, and it would be a failure of imagination not to draw on them at a moment like this. The Vedic notion of Rta, the order binding nature and human conduct into a seamless frame, and the Dharma that grew from it, never allowed human flourishing to be separated from the flourishing of the world that sustains it. 

Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, the conviction that the world is one family, was never sentiment reserved for ceremonial occasions but a working theory of interdependence long before ecologists spoke about it. These are not museum pieces. Mission Life, which Prime Minister Modi placed before the world at COP26 and carried further during India’s G20 presidency, translates that inheritance into policy, asking individuals and nations alike to examine consumption not as a private choice but as a collective responsibility. 

The principle of Antyodaya, beginning with the person standing last, and the practice of Janbhagidhari, making participation the method rather than the afterthought of development, are exactly the instruments a regenerative response to disasters like Rasuwa would need, because no early warning system, however sophisticated, replaces a community that knows its mountain well enough to read its moods. None of this argues against investment in infrastructure, forecasting, or the hard engineering that saves lives when disaster does strike. 

It argues that infrastructure alone, built on an unchanged relationship with the earth, will keep discovering the limits of its own insufficiency one collapsed glacier at a time. The nations gathering to reimagine the Goals beyond 2030 would do well to notice what Rasuwa and Guangxi are actually telling them, that resilience without renewal is a losing race against a warming planet, and that the country's best places to lead are not necessarily those with the largest budgets but those carrying the oldest, clearest memory of what it means to live in reciprocity with the earth rather than in extraction from it. 

India has that memory, and it has, in the same decade, the practical experience of lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty without needing to be told twice that development divorced from dignity is no development at all. That combination, ancient wisdom paired with recent, hard-won capability, is a rare inheritance, and it need not stay confined to conference halls and policy papers. 

Somewhere in the Himalayas right now, villagers who lost everything are already rebuilding, not with despair, but with the quiet, stubborn resolve that has carried mountain communities through worse. If a civilisation can find in that resolve the seed for a larger idea, that the work ahead is not merely to survive what the earth is enduring but to help it heal, then even a tragedy as raw as Rasuwa will have left behind something more durable than grief. It will have left a lesson the world is hopefully ready to learn. 
 

(The writer is Member, Niti Aayog. Views expressed are personal)

editorials.title: When Centurions sent Pattons to their graves
editorials.passage:
On September 1, the 1 Armoured Division commemorated the 60th anniversary of the Battle of Phillora in the Sialkot sector - one of the fiercest armoured engagements of the 1965 India-Pakistan war. Six decades later, Phillora remains etched in the memory of the Indian Army not merely as a contest between tanks, but as a story of bold leadership, professional skill and extraordinary courage in the face of formidable odds. 

The Pakistani Patton tanks were, by the standards of the time, among the most advanced armoured fighting vehicles in the region. Their technological superiority had created an aura of invincibility. Yet at Phillora, Indian Centurions demonstrated a lesson that remains relevant even in an age of precision weapons, drones and artificial intelligence: technology can provide an advantage, but it is human skill, leadership and determination that ultimately convert capability into combat power. 

That enduring legacy came alive at a commemorative so cial evening-cum-dinner organised by the Patiala Armoured Division. Among the most moving features of the gathering was the presence of octogenarian veterans - men who, as young officers and soldiers six decades ago, had faced those very Pattons across the battlefield. Their recollections were more than anecdotes. They were fragments of living history. 

As the veterans spoke, often with the humour and flourish that come naturally to those who have spent a lifetime recounting extraordinary experiences, the events of 1965 seemed to acquire a new immediacy. For the younger officers present, this was history without the distance of a textbook. These were the men who had actually been there. It was particularly heartening to see young officers listening with such attention. 

They were not merely paying courtesy to their seniors; they were engaging with a generation whose experiences remain relevant to the profession of arms. In an age of rapidly changing technology, the conversations served as a reminder that leadership, judgement, courage and camaraderie cannot be downloaded, automated or acquired overnight. For the veterans of Patiala, the occasion was equally meaningful. 

We remain grateful to the General Officer Commanding, Maj Gen P S Kanwar, for providing us the opportunity to remember and honour those who fought at Phillora. As the evening progressed, conversations naturally returned to the battle - the decisions that shaped it, the men who fought it and the sacrifices that made victory possible. At the centre of those recollections was the daring leadership of Maj Gen Rajindra Singh Sparrow and the battlefield valour of Lt Col Ardeshir Burzorji Tarapore, alongside the skill and determination of the armoured troops who fought in the Sialko t se ctor. 

Their actions demonstrated the importance of bold leadership under pressure and the ability to exploit opportunities amid the confusion and uncertainty of battle. The numbers associated with Phillora remain striking. Indian armoured formations inflicted heavy losses on Pakistani armour, including its much-vaunted Pattons, while Indian losses were limite d. Contemporary accounts record 67 enemy tanks destroyed or damaged against six Indian Centurions lost. But statistics, impressive as they are, tell only part of the story. 

A tank battle is ultimately fought by crews sealed inside steel, operating under extraordinary stress, uncertainty and danger. They must identify targets, make split-second decisions, manoeuvre, fire accurately and continue fighting despite knowing that every engagement can be fatal. The quality of the machine matters enormously, but so do training, discipline, leadership, morale and the ability to remain composed when everything around you is chaotic. 

That is perhaps the most enduring lesson of Phillora. It is also a lesson reflected elsewhere in the 1965 war. In the skies, the diminutive Gnat fighters earned the celebrate d sobriquet of ‘Sabre-slayers’ for their performance against Pakistan’s F-86 Sabres. Across land and air, Indian servicemen demonstrated that superior equipment does not automatically translate into battlefield superiority. The gallantry awards associated with the war provide another measure of the extraordinary courage displayed by India's armed forces. One Param Vir Chakra, four Maha Vir Chakras and seven Vir Chakras were awarded for acts of exceptional bravery during the conflict. 

Behind every decoration, however, was a human story-of fear overcome, duty placed above self, and comradeship sustained under the most difficult circumstances. There is another lesson in these stories that deserves to be remembered in today’s India. Courage does not belong to a caste, creed, religion or social class. On a battlefield, distinctions that may seem so important in ordinary life rapidly lose their meaning. What matters is whether the man beside you can be trusted, whether the leader can inspire confidence, and whether each individual is prepared to do his duty when circumstances demand it. 

British General Sir Edward Bruce Hamley captured something of this idea in his famous reflection on the flag: “A moth-eaten rag on a worm-eaten pole, it doesn’t look likely to stir a man’s soul; ’tis the deeds that were done ’neath the moth-eaten rag...” The words endure because symbols acquire meaning through the deeds of those who serve beneath them. Six decades after Phillora, India faces challenges very different from those of 1965. The battlefield has changed dramatically. 

Technology has transformed warfare, and the character of national power is increasingly shaped by economic strength, innovation, cyber capabilities, information and human capital. Yet the fundamental qualities required to meet adversity remain remarkably constant. Excellence, discipline, resilience, courage and a willingness to put the larger national interest above personal considerations are not merely military virtues. They are nation-building virtues. The young officers who listened to the veterans at Patiala therefore received something more valuable than a history lesson. 

They were reminded that every generation inherits not only institutions and equipment, but also a responsibility to preserve the values that enabled those institutions to endure. The Centurions that fought at Phillora are long gone from the battlefield. The men who commanded and crewed them are now in their eighties and beyond. Yet the spirit that carried them into battle has not become obsolete. The Centurions may have made a graveyard of Pattons at Phillora. Their greater achievement, however, was to leave behind a legacy of courage, leadership and unity. That is the legacy worth remembering - and passing on. 

(The writer is a retired Brigadier of the Indian Army and comments on strategic and international affairs.)

editorials.title: Why don’t we marry the same way?
editorials.passage:
In India, a wedding is rarely just the union of two people. It is a meeting of families, customs, languages, cuisines, histories and communities. This is why an Indian wedding can look completely different depending on where it takes place. A wedding in Kerala may have little resemblance to one in Punjab. A Bengali wedding may follow rituals unfamiliar to a Tamil family. A Christian wedding in Goa, a Muslim wedding in Hyderabad, a Sikh wedding in Amritsar or a tribal wedding in the Northeast may each have their own ceremonies, clothing and symbolism. Yet all of them are recognised as weddings. 

So why, in one nation, don’t we marry the same way? The simplest answer is that India was never culturally uniform. Its geographical size is only part of the explanation. Over centuries, different communities developed their own ways of understanding family, kinship, religion and social relationships. Marriage naturally became one of the strongest places where these identities were preserved. Geography played an important role. Different regions developed different foods, clothing, occupations and lifestyles, and wedding traditions evolved alongside them. 

Climate influenced clothing and cuisine. Agricultural communities developed ceremonies connected with harvests and seasons. Coastal communities developed food traditions shaped by access to seafood and tropical ingredients. Local flowers, grains and spices b ecame par t of wedding celebrations. History added another layer. India’s many kingdoms, migrations, trade routes and cultural exchanges created traditions that travelled, merged and changed. Communities moved across regions and carried their customs with them. Some traditions remained relatively local, while others spread widely. 

Religion also shaped married rituals, but even within the same religion there is enormous variation. Hindu weddings are perhaps the clearest example. A wedding in North India may prominently feature the pheras around the sacred fire, while a South Indian wedding may place greater emphasis on the tying of the thali or mangalsutra, exchange of garlands and rituals specific to the regional community. Bengali weddings include customs such as the bride’s ceremonial entrance and the shubho drishti, while Maharashtrian weddings have their own distinctive rituals and symbolism. 

There is no single “Indian Hindu wedding.” There are many. The same diversity exists beyond Hindu traditions. Muslim weddings vary significantly among regions and communities. Sikh weddings centre around the Anand Karaj ceremony, yet surrounding customs and celebrations can differ according to family and region. Christian weddings in India may combine church traditions with local customs, clothing and food. Then there are India’s tribal and indigenous communities, whose marriage traditions may be completely different from  mainstream  ceremonies. Some have distinctive dances, community participation , symbolic exchanges and traditional forms of matchmaking. 

This diversity tells us something important: marriage is not only a religious institution; it is also a cultural memory. When samples repeat a wedding ritual, they are often repeating what their grandparents and great grandparents did. A particular song may carry the language of a region. A piece of jewellery may represent a community’s history. A dish served at the wedding may have been prepared in the same family for generations. In that sense, weddings become living videos. 

But Indian weddings are changing. Urbanisation, inter-state marriages, migration and social media are creating increasingly hybrid celebrations. A couple may combine a traditional ceremony with a modern reception. A bride may wear a South Indian saree after for one ceremony and a North Indian lehenga for another. Families from different linguistic or religious backgrounds may deliberately combine their customs. Intercommunity marriages are therefore producing something new: the Indian fusion wedding. At the same time, modern weddings also raise questions about expense and social expectations. 

The pressure to organise increasingly elaborate celebrations can place financial burdens on families. The idea that weddings must be extravagant has been amplified by social media, celebrity culture and the wedding industry. Perhaps the challenge for modern India is not to make every wedding look the same, but to decide which traditions are worth preserving and which pressures are worth abandoning. A wedding does not become meaningful because it follows the same script as everyone else’s. 

Its meaning often comes from the traditions that make it personal. India’s wedding diversity therefore reflects something larger about the country itself. We have a national identity without having to erase regional identities. We can belong to one nation while speaking different languages, eating different food and celebrating different customs. That is why we don’t marry the same way. And perhaps we shouldn’t. India’s strength has never been its ability to make everyone identical. It has been its ability to allow different traditions to exist, evolve and sometimes come together. One nation. Many languages. Many cultures. And, naturally, many ways to say, “I do.” 

(The writer is a South-Korea based author and Doctor of Physiotherapy.)

editorials.title: The AI Bet
editorials.passage:
Silicon Valley has built a vast economic edifice on an assumption that remains surprisingly untested: that once artificial intelligence becomes sufficiently capable, almost everyone will use it as intensively as software engineers do. The assumption matters because extraordinary sums are being committed to make it possible. Technology companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centres, specialised chips and the electricity needed to run them. 

The investment is premised not merely on AI becoming useful, but on it becoming an indispensable and heavily consumed utility across the economy. So far, software developers offer the strongest proof that this can happen. AI coding assistants have moved rapidly from novelty to everyday tools. Engineers increasingly use AI to generate, debug and rewrite code, allowing a single worker to accomplish tasks that once required considerably more time. For technology companies, programmers are therefore the model customer: digitally sophisticated, frequent users whose work generates an obvious and measurable demand for computing power. But coders can supervise an AI system without surrendering professional responsibility for its mistakes. 

Many other occupations do not offer coding’s advantages. A lawyer cannot safely approve a contract merely because an AI system has produced convincing prose. A doctor cannot delegate clinical judgement to a chatbot. A corporate executive cannot blame an algorithm after an important negotiation goes wrong. In fields where mistakes carry legal, financial or human consequences, somebody must remain accountable. This may prove to be the central economic constraint on the AI revolution. The problem is no longer simply whether machines can perform tasks. 

Increasingly, they can. The harder question is whether institutions are willing to reorganise work around systems that remain imperfect and, in many cases, difficult to audit. That distinction should concern investors as much as workers. History offers ample warnings. The railways, electricity and the internet, all transformed economies but turned out to be spectacularly bad investment decisions. Being right about the future does not guarantee that today's valuations are right. The same may hold for AI. 

There is little reason to doubt that artificial intelligence will spread far beyond software engineering. It is already entering law, medicine, finance, marketing and administration. But widespread adoption is not the same as intensive use. An accountant who consults an AI assistant several times a day does not necessarily generate anything like the computing demand created by thousands of programmers constantly running sophisticated coding agents. 

The danger, therefore, is not an AI winter caused by technological failure. It is a mismatch between infrastructure built for explosive demand and an economy that adopts the technology more gradually. The great question confronting the AI industry is not whether people will use artificial intelligence. They undoubtedly will. It is whether enough of them will use enough of it, often enough, to pay for the colossal machinery now being built. That answer may determine whether the AI boom becomes an industrial revolution ~ or an infrastructure bubble.

editorials.title: Shared Peril
editorials.passage:
The catastrophic floods in Nepal should end a dangerous illusion in India: that Himalayan disasters can be neatly contained within national borders or explained simply by blaming an upstream neighbour for “releasing” water. The Himalayan river system does not recognise political boundaries. What happens in Nepal’s mountains can shape the fate of millions in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, just as infrastructure decisions on the Indian side can worsen flooding across Nepal’s Terai. 

The growing volatility of this shared ecosystem demands a fundamental shift from reactive disaster management to cooperative risk management. India has long treated floods largely as a domestic engineering problem, responding with embankments, barrages, relief camps and compensation. Yet the record suggests that controlling rivers is not the same as understanding them. The 2008 Kosi catastrophe remains an uncomfortable reminder. It was not simply an overwhelming volume of water that devastated Bihar; institutional failure and a breach in an inadequately maintained embankment transformed a manageable river flow into a humanitarian disaster. That distinction matters even more today. 

The Himalayas are producing hazards that increasingly defy the conventional definition of a flood. Cloudbursts, landslides, glacial lake outbursts and rock-and-ice avalanches can unleash torrents carrying enormous quantities of sediment and debris. The 2021 Chamoli disaster and the destruction at Dharali in Uttarakhand last year demonstrated the destructive potential of such events. Nepal’s latest tragedy belongs to the same expanding geography of Himalayan risk. 

Climate change compounds the problem, but invoking it should not become an excuse for institutional fatalism. A warming atmosphere may intensify extreme rainfall, yet human decisions determine much of the eventual damage. Roads and railways obstruct natural drainage; settlements expand across floodplains; embankments deteriorate; hydropower projects proliferate in fragile valleys; and warning systems often fail at the point where they matter most ~ reaching vulnerable communities in time. The India-Nepal relationship consequently needs a more ambitious framework than periodic exchanges of river data. Real-time monitoring must be expanded across vulnerable catchments. 

Joint forecasting models are needed, along with regular sharing of information on sediment movement, changing river channels, glacial lakes and the structural condition of embankments and barrages. Disaster warnings must also travel beyond government offices to the villages and households directly in harm’s way. This is not merely an environmental issue. North Bihar’s chronic vulnerability affects agriculture, migration, infrastructure and regional economic development. 

Repeated disasters can trap already poor communities in cycles of asset loss and displacement. The economic consequences of Himalayan instability will increasingly extend far beyond the mountains. The deeper lesson from Nepal is therefore one of interdependence. Neither country can engineer its way to safety independently while sharing rivers whose behaviour is becoming less predictable. The question is no longer whether the next Himalayan disaster will cross a border. It is whether the institutions on both sides will recognise that the border is largely irrelevant to the disaster itself.

editorials.title: A fading fire
editorials.passage:
On the morning of September 2, 1945, Japanese representatives signed the instrument of surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, formally ending the Second World War. Over eight decades later, the world’s promise of ‘Never Again’ to war looks thinner with each new conflict. Calcutta’s own reckoning with 1945 is, however, quieter and stranger.

For a city that has lived through empire, famine, Partition and rebellion, Calcutta has an oddly small acquaintance with war itself. Nearly every major city — London, Paris, Berlin, Tokyo, Moscow — has stood in conflict’s direct path. In roughly three centuries of its modern recorded history, Calcutta has felt war on its own soil only twice: in 1756, when Siraj-ud-Daulah took Fort William from the British, and between 1942 and 1944, when Japanese bombers reached the city. The second of these has almost vanished from our recent memory. This is odd because it happened alongside the event Bengal remembers most bitterly of all — the Bengal Famine.

By early 1942, Rangoon had fallen, and the Japanese advance through Burma had put Calcutta, the empire’s largest eastern port, within the bombers’ range, a threat that most other major Indian cities did not share. The first raids came on December 20, 1942, and continued till Christmas Eve, striking Kidderpore docks among other targets. A second, larger, daylight raid on December 5, 1943 hit the docks again, killing several hundred and cutting cargo capacity by two-thirds for weeks. Smaller raids continued all through 1944. An estimated 3,50,000 city residents fled in panic. Blackout drills, trenches dug through public squares, and air-raid sirens became part of the city’s daily life.

The bombing did not happen in isolation. It unfolded alongside the Bengal famine of 1943, and the two were more entangled than they first appear. The same fear of invasion that sent bombers over Kidderpore also drove Winston Churchill’s ‘denial policy’: the deliberate confiscation by the British of over 50,000 boats and surplus rice stocks from coastal Bengal was meant to deny an advancing Japanese army the means to move or feed itself. The British also implemented inflation policies during the war that were aimed at making more resources available for Allied troops. The denial policy, wartime procurement, inflation, disruption of rice supplies, cyclone and crop disease — all these miscalculations, layered on administrative failure and speculation — led to the death of close to 30 lakh people. The same military logic that turned Calcutta into a bombing target turned the Bengal countryside into an acute famine zone: both were the price extracted by the British administrators for defending the eastern frontier with the people living in it as collateral damage.

The images that survive of this moment mostly survive by accident, and mostly through foreign hands. Wartime censorship in colonial India was strict around military installations, ports, railway stations, and troop movements, precisely the subjects that mattered most in Calcutta during the war. Indian newspapers and photographers worked under immense press restrictions that made it risky, often impossible, to photograph the docks, the damage, life in the city and in the suburbia, or the famine’s toll. Thus very few indigenous photographic records of these years survive.

What exists instead comes largely from foreign servicemen-cum-photographers who had military clearance to be near the docks, railway stations, and the barracks and were allowed to photograph the city streets. Consequently, two American photographers — they were not part of the Indian press — ended up producing what may be the fullest surviving visual account of Calcutta during the Second World War.

Glenn S. Hensley (June 3, 1919 — January 23, 2018) was one such American serviceman who served in the 40th Army Photography Reconnaissance and was in British India between 1943 and 1945. Along with the official images he captured for the United States army, Hensley produced a series of personal photographs portraying his immediate surroundings and his experience of life during the Second World War in British India and in Burma. He had photographed Calcutta while the danger of war was very real, between 1943 and 1944. He gave away nearly 600 images to the University of Chicago Library where they now form the ‘Hensley Collection’, digitised through the Digital South Asia Library. Despite the size of his wartime contribution, Hensley remains almost absent in Calcutta’s historical writings and museums and from our memory — an odd fate for his unique photographic record of the city was taken during , not after , its brush with the active years of the Second World War.

Clyde Waddell (June 20, 1915 — February 11, 1997) came to Calcutta slightly later. He was a bit more fortunate than Hensley. A Houston Press photographer inducted into the US army, Waddell was attached in November 1943 to the Public Relations Staff of South East Asia Command: a joint Allied, British-led command under Louis Mountbatten but staffed by Americans and British alike. Waddell served as Mountbatten’s personal photographer before moving to the Phoenix magazine, a picture weekly run jointly by both commands. Waddell took his own Calcutta photographs while on leave in 1945 after the bombing had stopped. They include Chowringhee’s trams, the Burra Bazar, Nimtolla’s crematorium, opium dens in Tiretta Bazaar, GIs mixing with street vendors near the Tipu Masjid at Dharmatala crossing and the famine-stricken mother and child. Friends kept asking for copies until he self-published 60 of his photographs as A Yank’s Memories of Calcutta in 1946. It’s often called a nearly lost book, but that isn’t quite right: documented copies survive at the University of Pennsylvania, Southeastern Louisiana University and the British Library besides others that have surfaced at auction over the years. Rare, yes; vanished, no; just scattered widely enough such that few people, in Calcutta or anywhere else, have seen it whole. However, his photographs have been plagiarised and reconfigured by social media influencers in recent times.

Between them, the two men left behind something rare: one captured the city’s fear, one its exhaled relief, months apart. Almost nobody alive remembers the sirens first hand now; what’s left is second-hand: a grandparent’s mention of trenches near a school, a scarred building in old Dalhousie Square, a photograph nobody in the family can quite place. That is usually how Calcutta’s war memory ends: not with an event, but with the slow disappearance of anyone who can say ‘I was there’.

Apart from Hensley and Waddell, there were at least three other American servicemen photographers — Frank Bond, Lewis Paltz, and Tony Mayo who had photographed wartime Bengal.

Calcutta is unusual among world cities for having so little war in its past. It is more unusual still for having let the one real brush it did have — bombed docks, a starving population, and a city in churn — slip almost entirely out of its own telling or memory. Part of the reason is geography: the Hensley Collection sits in Chicago, Waddell’s album is scattered across libraries and auction rooms abroad, and no Indian museum, archive or university, to the best of my knowledge, holds a complete set of either.

Recovering that record now is not nostalgia; it would mean bringing digitised copies home so that every Calcuttan can finally see what almost nobody photographed from the inside, before the last people who could say, ‘I was there’, are gone.

Devasis Chattopadhyay is a narrative history writer and columnist

editorials.title: Asaduddin Owaisi’s AIMIM ‘B team’ tag resurfaces as aide joins Congress
editorials.passage:
In Delhi’s political circles, the All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen, led by the Hyderabad member of Parliament, Asaduddin Owaisi, is often portrayed as the Bharatiya Janata Party’s ‘B team’ — an allegation the party has repeatedly rejected. The charge resurfaced after the AIMIM spokesperson, Syed Asim Waqar, considered close to Owaisi, crossed over to the Congress. Waqar justified his move by alleging that while the AIMIM claims to oppose the BJP, its electoral tactics end up hurting anti-BJP forces. Owaisi has long faced allegations that his party fields candidates in key state elections to split the anti-BJP vote, particularly among Muslims. Yet, Owaisi has emerged as one of the BJP’s most articulate and combative critics, frequently targeting the prime minister, Narendra Modi, the BJP and the wider sangh parivar. He recently turned Modi’s latest foreign honour from Uzbekistan — the country’s highest State award for foreign nationals — into a powerful political barb. Congratulating Modi, Owaisi pointed out that the honour came from the country of Babur, the Mughal founder, repeatedly vilified as a foreign invader by the saffron ecosystem. “Babur belonged to the Fergana Valley in present-day Uzbekistan. The country from which he came is now honouring you,” Owaisi said, urging the sangh parivar to reflect on the irony and reconsider its rhetoric on Babur.

At the joint media briefing with Narendra Modi, the Belgian PM, Bart De Wever, revealed that his gift for his Indian counterpart had melted. He said, “I had actually planned to present to Prime Minister Modi a fitting gift — a sculpture of India Gate entirely made out of the best Belgian chocolates. But unlike the real India Gate, which has stood for almost a century, the chocolate version didn’t even survive the journey to India.” The choice of the colonial memorial to Indian soldiers who fell in the Great War, said De Wever, was a tribute to their sacrifice for his country. “On the sculpture, the chocolate version, we enlarged a part of the inscription that commemorates Indian soldiers who fought and fell in Flanders Fields during the First World War.”

Sujata Rout Karthikeyan — she is a former civil servant and the wife of VK Pandian, a close aide of the former chief minister of Odisha, Naveen Patnaik — has sparked a political storm in Odisha with a powerful article in Odia on the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2026. Karthikeyan warned that the state’s economy faces severe setbacks due to the Odisha government’s failure to collect mining tax arrears owed by companies. She pointed out that despite the Supreme Court in 2024 permitting the recovery of arrears, the state government did not act to collect them. She estimated that Odisha stands to lose nearly one lakh crore rupees in unpaid dues from mining companies, along with an annual revenue loss exceeding Rs 12,000 crore. She also questioned the silence of BJP MPs on the issue. Her aggressive tone has caught state BJP leaders off guard. By combining bureaucratic authority with political sharpness, Karthikeyan has placed the state BJP government on the defensive.

The noted lawyer, Vrinda Grover, recently found herself in the spotlight after representing the Cockroach Janta Party in the Supreme Court. But a news article featuring a photograph of the senior advocate, Indira Jaisingh, became the subject of discussion on social media when a right-wing account mistook Jaisingh for Grover. Grover was tagged in a post carrying an article about the CBI raid on Jaisingh’s office and claimed, “queen of all cockroaches, Vrinda Grover’s FCRA licence got cancelled in 2016”. The post went viral with many critiquing the account for spreading a false narrative. The post also drew Grover’s attention, prompting her to quote the account and write: “How did he manage to get everything wrong?”

The recent move of the Congress to end its ties with the Raijor Dal, citing a breach of alliance ethics, was not unexpected. The alliance appeared uninspiring from the outset and cracks began to show soon after the six-party Opposition alliance’s debacle in the April assembly polls. But the Congress’s worry is far from over. The Nagaon Lok Sabha by-polls, which were necessitated because the sitting Congress MP joined the ruling BJP just before the state polls, are looming. However, Congress insiders are happy with the break-up with Raijor Dal but said the party appears “extremely bereft of ideas, energy, and cohesion” since losing the state polls. With many Congress leaders joining the BJP and the Assam PCC president and sitting Jorhat MP, Gaurav Gogoi, having to divide his time between Delhi and Assam, they claim that hardly any leader is making an impact.

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: The cruelty concealed by sentimental talk about man’s best friend
editorials.passage:
Sir — The domestication of wolves began a symbiotic relationship in which humans and dogs hunted together and offered each other protection. That bond has since become deeply unequal. A biotechnology firm now claims to have created hypoallergenic dogs through gene editing, despite the risk of unintended consequences. Humans have, in effect, edited dog genes for centuries through selective breeding, leaving many animals prone to disease and deformity. The dachshund’s damaged back and the pug’s breathing difficulties expose the cruelty concealed by sentimental talk about man’s best friend.

Sir — The author, Su. Ven­katesan, has rightly observed that literature shaped by history often has a more en­during impact than conventional historical writing (“Stories and histories”, Sept 5). History records what happened; literature draws upon the past to illuminate the present. In acclaimed works such as Kaaval Kottam and Velpari , Venkatesan places contemporary lives and struggles against historical backdrops. For him, retelling history is a political and cultural act that connects inherited traditions with present realities. Political work may offer immediate relief but literature can influence public consciousness for generations.

Sir — History and literature are distinct academic disciplines: history is concerned with fact, while literature frequently draws upon imagination. Yet, G.M. Trevelyan had described them as inseparable twin sisters. Poetry and prose cannot be fully appreciated without some knowledge of the period from which they emerged. Literary works contain allusions to the social and the political circumstances of their times, even when they address universal themes. An understanding of the past therefore deepens the reading of literature.

Tapan Kumar Mukherjee, Burdwan

Sir — The Supreme Court’s decision to quash first information reports against the youth involved in the Cockroach Janta Party protests is commendable. By invoking Article 142 to deliver “complete justice”, the court has protected thousands of young people from the lasting consequences of criminal records. The protests arose from legitimate anger over examination failures and paper leaks. As the court observed, participation in a public demonstration is not a criminal offence. Its direction to formulate a nationwide compensation policy for bereaved families of NEET students is equally welcome. Student unrest demands reform and understanding, rather than indiscriminate criminalisation.

Ranganathan Sivakumar, Chennai

Sir — The apex court’s use of its special powers to quash cases filed by the Delhi Police against young protesters at Jantar Mantar and elsewhere is welcome. It reaffirms the democratic right to protest against the State. Subjecting peaceful protesters to criminal cases merely because some miscreants infiltrate a gathering is unjust. The court has corrected this indiscriminate approach and restored the confidence of law-abiding young citizens raising legitimate concerns.

D.V.G. Sankara Rao, Andhra Pradesh

Sir — Teachers shape young minds, encourage lifelong learning and guide pupils through their conduct as well as their words. The growing use of Artificial Intelligence in classrooms has raised questions about the future of teaching. Technology, however, cannot replicate a teacher’s capacity to form emotional connections. Teachers help young people become independent thinkers, compassionate individuals and responsible citizens. Their role will remain indispensable.

M. Jeyaram, Sholavandan, Tamil Nadu

editorials.title: Brightest star: Editorial on Uttam Kumar at 100 and Bengali cinema’s revival
editorials.passage:
The centennial birth celebrations of Uttam Kumar, still the brightest star in Bengal’s celluloid universe, have begun, expectedly, with a flurry of activities. The chief minister, surrounded by members of Bengal’s film clan, took part in a tribute and a procession. An exhibition, comprising publicity material and music albums of the films of the matinee idol, was inaugurated at the Gaganendra Pradarshashala. Nandan organised a three-day film retrospective, while India Post released a special cover. Far more intimate and illuminating, though, have been the reminiscences, mostly by veterans who shared slices of real and reel life with the legend. These have shone a spotlight, once again, on various aspects of the actor’s persona. For instance, his steely resolve to succeed after suffering the ignominy of a series of flops, his endeavour to improve his craft, the phenomenal success that followed, his productive cinematic partnership with Suchitra Sen, his subsequent forays into Hindi cinema, his quiet solidarity with those in need, his troubled personal life and health, undiminished professionalism — the actor suffered his fatal heart attack on a film set — each aspect of the mahanayak ’s life continues to be dissected passionately in Bengal.

This feverish fascination lays bare a question for which there are many answers — but, arguably, not a definite one. What are the ingredients of Uttam Kumar’s hypnotic appeal? His natural charm and progression as an actor —the versatility of his roles testifies to the latter — offer some clues. Others would suggest that the icon defined, for generations, the contours of both civility and masculinity, a masculinity that was not turbocharged by brawn but by intelligence, refinement and relatability. His ability to represent a quintessential middle-class Bengaliness — with its attendant values, aspirations, moorings — is perhaps the most accurate reason for the hero’s perpetual aura in the public eye. Yet, Uttam Kumar’s Bengali essence, so central to his unmatched success in the state, did, some suggest, turn out to be his Achilles heel in the world of Hindi films. There is a line of thought that suggests that Chhoti Si Mulaqat , which Uttam Kumar produced and which was a Hindi remake of the Bengali superhit, Agnipariksha , failed miserably because of the cultural chasm that separated the then Bengal from Bombay. That failure had adversarial financial and health consequences for Bengal’s first —and only? — superstar.

Uttam Kumar’s 100th birth anniversary would certainly open the proverbial dam on imaginative and not-so-imaginative tributes. Perhaps the best way to honour the man would be for all stakeholders — the film fraternity, the government and the audience, among others — to try and revive the fortunes of Bengali cinema. In this respect, content needs a radical resurrection in terms of quality so that the ordinary Bengali would return to the sparsely populated cinema halls. Such a sorry sight — a theatre with a handful of people in the audience — would have been unthinkable during Uttam Kumar’s heyday.

editorials.title: Editorial. Gaming children
editorials.passage:
Meta’s reported $18 billion US settlement, and its agreement to implement sweeping safety guardrails for young American users, exposes a glaring corporate double standard. While Meta moves to introduce mandatory two-hour daily caps, overnight usage blocks, and non-algorithmic feeds in the US, it has offered no such protections to Indian children, despite India being its largest single market by user base.

This cynical asymmetry should force an immediate reckoning for Indian policymakers. Reports and litigation in the US have alleged that Meta knew about the addictive potential of features built into its platforms, and yet continued to use design tools that maximise engagement. This reinforces the case for Indian regulators to examine whether children are being exposed to products deliberately engineered to keep them engaged. Autoplay, endless scrolling, personalised feeds, notifications and algorithmic recommendations can turn casual use into compulsive behaviour, particularly among children whose capacity for self-regulation is still developing.

The Centre should commission an independent, evidence-based study into the impact of platforms such as Meta’s Instagram and Facebook on children and adolescents. This should examine not merely screen time but the effects of algorithmic recommendations, addictive design, exposure to harmful content, online harassment and social comparison. If the evidence establishes that platforms have knowingly deployed design features that cause demonstrable harm to children, they should be held accountable. India cannot allow global technology companies to treat its vast young user base as a market in which the social costs of their business models are someone else’s problem. The Centre has summoned social-media executives, issued warnings and expressed concern. But it has rarely gone beyond exhortation.

Whether it was the controversy over the misuse of personal data by data-analytics firms, the continuing challenge of child sexual abuse material on platforms such as Instagram, or the broader question of children’s access to social media, the response has too often stopped at warnings, meetings and consultations. The Centre has been discussing the possibility of regulating children’s access to social media, but discussion cannot substitute for policy. Australia has already moved to restrict social-media access for children under 16. The Economic Survey has pointed towards regulating the architecture of platforms themselves. Teen-safe defaults, stronger privacy protections, tighter controls on messaging and recommendations, and disabling features such as autoplay for young users should be considered. Platforms should also face meaningful transparency and accountability obligations, allowing regulators to scrutinise how their algorithms affect children. The fact that Meta has agreed to build safeguards in the US proves that these features are technically buildable. For too long, India has relied on voluntary compliance. It is time that regulation takes over.

Published on September 4, 2026

editorials.title: Off the record by P Vaidyanathan Iyer: The economy, its math and politics
editorials.passage: The government machinery was on an overdrive the last few days responding to one former bureaucrat who wrongly debunked the robust growth estimates for April-June 2026. The bureaucrat, Subhash Chandra Garg, was the Economic Affairs Secretary in the Ministry of Finance for over two years from June 2017 to July 2019, and was designated the Finance Secretary in his last four months in the ministry. The Finance Secretary is the ‘first among equals’ in the Ministry which has six secretaries now, each heading one of the six departments — Expenditure, Revenue, Economic affairs, Financial Services, Investment and Public Asset Management, and Public Enterprises. The government was spooked after Garg claimed in an interview to a television channel (NDTV) and later wrote in a piece for an online site (thequint.com) that the nominal GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth rate in the first quarter of 2026-27 was a ‘lowly’ 2.6 per cent, and not 10.3 per cent as estimated by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. Adjusted for 2-2.5 per cent inflation, he claimed the real growth rate will be zero and not the ‘designer number’ 7.8 per cent estimated by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI). In doing so, Garg did something egregious. He definitely knows better than this, having played a key role in pushing through some of the most controversial agendas in the first term of the Narendra Modi government such as electoral bonds for political funding, and higher surplus transfers from RBI to the Centre. He elaborates on both these issues in his book We Also Make Policy. ALSO READConflict over Cauvery Everybody got Garg’s wrong maths, but what also matters in the street is perception. Garg’s claims, though misleading, resonated with some coming as they did in the backdrop of the Jantar Mantar protests, an education system that admittedly does not leave its graduates ‘job ready’, and a demography which pushes more than a crore youth into the job market every year. Not surprising then, the Congress and some of its leaders pounced on this and amplified it. But what is surprising is that Rahul Gandhi, who is a strong critic of the economic policies of the Narendra Modi government, chose prudently not to comment on Garg’s claims. His silence was loud and meant wrong maths can’t be defended. Rajya Sabha member Praveen Chakravarty, hit out at the government’s economic management, but said in a piece for The New Indian Express that “there is a lot that is wrong with India’s economy… but the sheer math behind the 7.8 per cent real GDP growth is not one of them, contrary to what a former government bureaucrat has claimed”. But Subhash Garg did leave the government firefighting much of the week after the GDP estimates were released. To reject what he said, it is key to understand two concepts: i) why is a base year needed while calculating GDP growth rate, and ii) why is the base year changed once in every 5-6 years, and when this is done, how is GDP calculated. ALSO READWho are you, again? CONCEPT 1: Need for a base year. Simply put, a base year is needed to understand if the economy or the GDP has indeed grown, adjusting for the impact of price rise. For example, let's assume Country X produces only crude oil, so the market value of its crude oil becomes its GDP. Say, in year 1, it produces 10 million barrels of crude oil and sells it for $10 a barrel; its GDP will be $100 million (10 million barrels X 10/ barrel). In year 2, it produces only 5 million barrels, and oil prices have risen to $30 a barrel. So, its GDP will be $150 million (5 million barrels X 30/ barrel). So, even though the country has produced less oil, its GDP has risen 50 per cent from $100 million to $150 million. A base year helps tell the real GDP growth by removing the impact of prices. If year 1 is taken as the base year, the oil price of that year becomes the reference for the following years. So, the real GDP of year 2 will be $50 million (5 million barrels x $10 a barrel, which is the price of crude oil per barrel in the base year). So, in this example, the GDP has shrunk by 50% to $50 million from $100 million. CONCEPT 2: Why the base year is changed. Products and services on which people spend money today, be it food and clothes or travel and entertainment, has changed significantly from a decade ago. As years roll by, the market value of products and services change. So does technology and methodology, that enable a more precise and fast capture of output and prices. The base year is changed to account for all these. And when the base year changes, the GDP values naturally change, and growth is calculated by considering the new GDP values of two comparable periods. When MoSPI changed the base year from 2011-12 to 2022-23 in February this year, the GDP values changed for all years from 2011-12 till date. Garg took the GDP value of April-June 2025 calculated using the 2011- 12 base year and the GDP value of April-June 2026 calculated using the 2022-23 base year, to calculate the first quarter GDP growth rate for this year. Using numbers from two different series is patently wrong. The writer is Managing Editor, The Indian Express. Off the Record is a fortnightly column

editorials.title: Inside Track by Coomi Kapoor: Outsiders unwelcome
editorials.passage: Diplomatic insiders in both Delhi and Bangladesh see a powerful lobby in the external affairs ministry playing a part in thwarting efforts to bring about a rapprochement in Indo-Bangladesh ties. The MEA is perhaps upset over Modi’s appointment of a non-IFS officer, politician Dinesh Trivedi, as India’s High Commissioner to Bangladesh. In a meeting with Indian envoys earlier this year, Modi hinted at more non-IFS ambassadorial appointments in our neighbourhood. Trivedi’s efforts at bridging the growing gulf between the neighbours, even persuading Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman to agree to dates for a visit to India, was not appreciated by all. After the dates leaked, the MEA acted as a spoiler. Ignoring conventional foreign policy protocol, it permitted Sheikh Hasina to hold a virtual press conference at Delhi’s Foreign Correspondents Club, where she attacked her country’s government. (It is pertinent to note that a year ago, the MEA stymied a proposed Hasina press conference at the Delhi Press Club and in 2018, denied permission to a British emissary to speak on behalf of late Khaleda Zia, then jailed in Bangladesh. Belatedly, two weeks after a Hasina press conference, when the FCC tried to organise a foreign policy seminar which had speakers with alleged Awami League links, the government ordered its cancellation and some 50 policemen descended on the club premises!) ALSO READConflict over Cauvery Incidentally, the MEA’s non-conciliatory tone is echoed by some former Indian diplomats in articles, suggesting Rahman’s visit was in fact called off because of internal differences within Bangladesh over its foreign policy direction towards India. Embittered feelings on both sides indicate Rahman is unlikely to attend the BRICS summit in Delhi. Divisions at home The Home Ministry is on the backfoot after the police overreach towards CJP student protesters. However, just a month after the much-criticised July police crackdown, Cabinet Secretary Dr T V Somanathan and Home Secretary Govind Mohan, who were both due to retire this month, were given a year’s extension. The extensions are believed to reflect the PM’s appreciation of the two senior officials’ mature decision to refuse to succumb to political pressure that called for more stringent action during the Jantar Mantar agitation. The Home Secretary reportedly helped salvage the situation by halting the firing of pellets, a draconian measure which backfired badly. He was backed by the Cabinet Secretary. The Delhi Police’s harsh methods were adopted within three days of the abrupt transfer of commissioner Satish Golcha, who was replaced by Anurag Kumar, the Intelligence Bureau special director, in the belief that his background would help in dispersing the restive students. In fact, the reverse happened, the confrontation escalated. A fallout of the Jantar Mantar debacle is that officials are increasingly requesting for written ministerial orders. Unfair clubbing together BJP MPs who decry what they term as Delhi’s Lutyens culture have little sympathy for the government’s eviction notice to the Gymkhana Club. They think club culture is perpetrated to make those excluded feel like lesser mortals. A minister recalls when he came to Delhi years ago as a visitor in connection with a case in the Supreme Court, he was taken by his lawyer to the India International Centre for tea. He was made to feel like an outsider and suspected it was because he did not speak in English. His prejudice against the IIC may be misconceived, and the comparison unfair. The IIC membership criteria is based on a prospective candidate’s professional accomplishments and an interest in foreign affairs, while the complaint against the Gymkhana is its entrenched hereditary membership and elitism. ALSO READWho are you, again? Non-Parsis' exclusion There was an interesting subplot in the tussle for control of the Tata empire. Some months ago, when then trustee Mehli Mistry raised the issue of the 1923 deed of the Bai Hirabai Tata Charitable Foundation, which stipulates that all trustees should be Parsis, the assumption was that he was merely targeting the two non-Parsi trustees, Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh. But some Parsis suspected he might also be hinting at Noel Tata. As Naval Tata’s son, Noel’s Parsi credentials should be impeccable, but a few old-timers quibbled that Noel’s late mother, nee Simone Dunoyer, was a Christian. They could not recall a young Noel’s navjote ceremony, the initiation rite for being inducted into the faith. In fact, there is no ambiguity about Noel’s standing as a Parsi. Before his marriage to tycoon Shapoorji Pallonji Mistry’s daughter, Aloo, the conservative and deeply religious Shapoorji insisted that his prospective son-in-law go through the navjote ritual before the wedding.

editorials.title: The world is being driven to the brink by thugs and dictators, but there is a route to a brighter future
editorials.passage:
D on’t look up! The world is a mess. The sky could fall in any day. Unending wars, expanding humanitarian crises, rising authoritarianism, dysfunctional democracies, rampant racial and religious extremism, and unchecked lawlessness cast a dark cloud as the west’s new political year begins. Set all that against a backdrop of staggering global economic inequality, corporate and individual greed, irresponsible government indebtedness, dangerous AI gambles, climate breakdown and proliferating nuclear weapons, and a truly apocalyptic global outlook begins to take shape. It’s enough to make anyone shut their eyes, cover their ears and utter a Munch-like scream. And it’s only getting worse.

Democratic leaders who promise a better, safer, more optimistic future – what Britain’s freshly arrived prime minister, Andy Burnham, calls a “ new era of possibility ” – cannot escape this wider international context. Last week’s global bond market upheaval , sparked by external factors, left Burnham’s cash-strapped government struggling with sharply increased borrowing costs before he barely got started. The fact he chose Ukraine for his first overseas trip, while symbolically important, highlighted another grim reality. As a lead opponent of Vladimir Putin’s invasion, Britain now finds itself in a de facto state of war with Russia – and facing attack. Argentina, too, is eyeing UK defence vulnerabilities . These are not the sort of possibilities Burnham envisaged.

Little wonder some analysts believe a third world war has already begun. Those who say this is over-dramatic should consider the following snapshots of the state of the world in 2026. From Kyiv to Khorramshahr, Kordofan and Kachin, conflicts flare and subside but never seem to end. All-out Russian aggression in Ukraine, now mostly comprising daily attempts to murder and terrorise civilians, is into its fifth year. Trump has lost his Iran bet, but keeps killing and bombing with no end in sight. In southern Sudan , appalling atrocities go unchecked. In Myanmar, a people’s war against a brutal junta rages on. Israel’s response to the 2023 massacres has triggered an ongoing regional war embroiling Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Iran and the Gulf states. Worldwide, record numbers of people are displaced by conflict.

Increasingly interconnected, these wars threaten to merge into one uncontrollable global conflagration. The alliance system, key pillar of the post-1945 order, is eating itself. Donald Trump taunts Europe and Nato with tariffs, troop withdrawals, barbs and insults at a time of acute vulnerability. Canada and the US are at daggers drawn as the White House bully fatuously threatens Venezuela – or Greenland-style annexation. China aids North Korea , which also aids Russia, which aids Iran, which aids Hezbollah and the Houthis. In Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia, China looms menacingly as partnerships with Washington fray. In Taiwan, fears of invasion grow, aggravated by Trump’s obsequious appeasing of Xi Jinping .

Everywhere you look, humanitarian crises caused by war, the climate crisis or natural disasters are producing chaotic mass migrations, malnutrition and disease. Increasingly, the suffering overwhelms a UN-led aid system crippled by US and UK funding cuts. In the fertile West Bank, 900,000 Palestinians , their homes and farms besieged by settler extremists, are now food insecure, the World Food Programme says. In Somalia, millions go hungry amid record drought and predicted El Niño-related flooding. Colombia and Afghanistan face similar perils. Humanitarian and human rights outrages take individual form, too. In Hong Kong, for example, an ailing Jimmy Lai , brave champion of free speech, languishes in 23-hour-a-day solitary confinement, a tortured casualty of Chinese communism’s hatred of democracy and civil rights.

Skittish bond markets may be the least of the world’s economic and financial problems. Is a crash coming, reminiscent of 2008, only worse? The signs are ominous. The US just notched up a record $40tn in national debt . France, the UK, Japan and others are deep in the red, too. Unmanageable current-account deficits, rising inflation and the huge, draining diversion of investment into bloated AI tech companies all point to what market analysts cutely call a “disorderly correction”. By some estimates, the Nvidia chip-maker, plus Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft, are “worth” about 23% of the entire US stock market . Meanwhile, unaffordable northern-hemisphere energy and food prices loom this winter, exacerbated by Trump’s Middle East forever folly. In the worst case, all this could translate into global recession and yet more political instability. It’s a gigantic bubble waiting to burst.

The existential hazards posed by the climate crisis and global heating should require scant elaboration after the terrifying Nepal-Tibet flood disaster . Similarly inimical to life on Earth, in an avoidable, human-made way, is the rapid proliferation of nuclear weapons, including so-called “battlefield” or tactical nukes that are more likely to be used in war zones such as Ukraine or Iran. All nine nuclear weapons states are expanding or modernising their arsenals, with China in the lead . Countries such as South Korea and Saudi Arabia weigh their nuclear options. And now this atomic arms race is expanding into space. There really seems no limit to humanity’s relentless, doom-laden drive towards self-destruction.

The fundamental values of post-Enlightenment liberal societies are everywhere under siege. The rule of law is routinely flouted. While Putin and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu ignore war-crimes arrest warrants, Trump and his unctuous lickspittle, Marco Rubio , actively work to destroy the international criminal court. Across Europe, far-right racists, loons and bigots make political advances, seen again this weekend in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt . Next year, France will approach its own fateful national reckoning. In the US, Trump, enabled by a supine majority in Congress and dishonourable supreme court justices, is constructing a “ constitutional dictatorship ” to subvert future elections, symbolised by a gross, 250ft-tall “ Arc de Trump ”. Let alarm bells ring: US democracy and the entire western democratic tradition are in dire peril.

What is to be done? Is any consolation to be had? First, key pillars of the post-1945 order, though badly battered, are still just about intact. The UN and most of its agencies, the international court of justice and collaborative, multinational western democratic alliances such as the EU, Nato and the G7 have so far survived the current tumult. Second, the age of tyrants is nearing an end. These angry old men are mostly headed for nursing homes, jail or the grave. May their legacies of fear and hate die with them. Last, younger generations in many “middle power” and developing countries, exemplified by India’s Cockroach youth protest movement , are making plain their revulsion and rejection of the way the world is now. Like Burnham, they believe passionately in the power of possibility and change.

The future lies not in the hands of political thugs and killers, of dictators and megalomaniacs, but in the hands of ordinary people everywhere. It depends on millions upon millions of individual daily acts of kindness, selflessness, faith and courage. So don’t lose heart. Keep your eyes open. Unblock your ears. And don’t look down!

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

editorials.title: Aged 41, I’m back at my secondary school – but this time they’ve let me in the staffroom
editorials.passage:
Y ou know those dreams when you’re back at school? And you’re sitting at a desk reading a GCSE exam paper? Only you don’t recognise anyone around you? Well, I am living that dream. Because, at the age of 41, I have gone back to school. And not just any school. I have gone back to my own secondary school. Only this time, I am allowed in the staffroom.

That’s right: a short 25 years after walking out of those concrete and carpeted halls, the smell of polyester jumpers and canteen chips heady on the early summer air, I am back. But now I’m training to be a teacher.

To some extent, this was inevitable due to the logistics of my life. Despite a few lessons, I have never learned to drive (my instructor asked my mum out on a date and things got so awkward so quickly I have never really been behind a steering wheel since). I also have small children at nursery and primary school nearby, which meant that I had to beg my training scheme to place me at a school I could easily cycle to.
