But as I sit beneath the very ceiling tiles I once knew as intimately as the freckles on my own arm, I also wonder if this was somehow destined. If I, as someone who loved school, was raised by a teacher, and married a teacher who was himself raised by a teacher, was always going to join the family business. Or if, like one of those eels that swims all the way from the silty bed of some Essex river out to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, only for its larvae to wriggle all 10,000 salty kilometres back home, I have been slowly making my way back to school since I left.

It is undeniably odd to find myself walking across the playground on which I first tasted Um Bongo, and heard the name the Strokes , and hid my first love bite under a sticky layer of foundation. As I hustle to a safeguarding meeting, or am escorted by my mentor to pick up my new printing code, I can’t help but remember treading that same route at 15, wearing a skirt I’d sewn myself out of wetsuit material (I stretched the definition of our school uniform back then until the seams screamed), or with the initials of the boy I fancied written in ballpoint pen on the inside of my thumb, or on the way to my last ever chemistry lesson.

I’m also far from the only person I know hole-punching their way into a new career after decades in the arts, media or what we used to laughingly call “the creative industries”. I can count at least four former journalists from my contingent retraining as English teachers, another who is well on their way to qualifying as a plumber, a DJ working as a midwife, and a fair crop of writers, poets and journalists working towards jobs as therapists.

The old story used to be that ambitious people worked as teachers for a few years and then went into creative fields – Romesh Ranganathan , Philip Pullman , Joanne Harris , Greg Davies and so on. But it seems to me that publishing, music, broadcasting and all the rest are now losing scores of mid-career artists to the world of education and other public services. Or rather, if you’re lucky, the ambition to press your thumb on to the surface of the world, through writing or performing, one day gives way to a far greater urge: to unfurl the thousands of brilliant minds coming up behind you.

I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic moulded chairs, as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders. I am thrilled at the prospect of being able to dissect a novel over weeks in a classroom, rather than in minutes on the radio. I am delighted to be back in my old assembly hall, taking notes on a lined page, only this time with grey hairs, and two children down the road, and two decades of life in my rucksack.

And this time I don’t even need to bring in my PE kit.

Nell Frizzell is a journalist and author

editorials.title: Mansour Abbas is betting on a Zionist to make Palestinian votes count
editorials.passage:
When Raam leader Mansour Abbas appeared alongside former Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovich this week and announced that Segalovich would run second on the party’s electoral slate, much of the immediate attention went to the obvious novelty: An Israeli Jewish politician, openly Zionist and a former police major-general, running near the top of the list of a conservative Islamist Arab party. That combination is unusual, and it was meant to look unusual.

Jewish participation in political lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel is not, in itself, unprecedented. Hadash was built around a Jewish-Arab political tradition and has for decades included Jewish candidates and lawmakers. Ofer Cassif sits in the Knesset today as one of its most outspoken Jewish members. What is distinctive about the Abbas-Segalovich arrangement is not that a Jew is running with an Arab list. It is the kind of Jewish political voice Abbas has chosen to place there: a Zionist former senior police commander whose political biography sits comfortably inside the Israeli mainstream, not outside it.

Segalovich is joining Raam’s slate, not Raam itself, and the difference is easy to miss if one stops at the photograph. According to the arrangement, he will join the electoral list and parliamentary faction but will not become a member of the party. Raam’s constitution and internal decision-making structure will not change. Segalovich is also expected to retain the freedom to vote independently on questions where the ideological distance is obvious, including religion and state, security and LGBTQ rights. Abbas is not converting Raam into a Zionist party and Segalovich is not becoming an Islamist. They are testing whether two political identities that remain quite far apart can inhabit the same electoral vehicle.

I am not convinced that the main purpose of the move is electoral, at least not in the simple sense of adding more votes. Segalovich may bring some. An August Channel 13 poll suggested that a slate including him could perform somewhat better than Raam has in other surveys, and he retains unusual credibility among Arab local leaders because of his work on organised crime while serving as deputy public security minister in coalition governments led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.

In that period he became one of the few senior Jewish officials associated in Arab public memory not only with promises about crime, but with a governmental programme that actually tried to confront it. That helps Abbas now, when criminal violence remains one of the most immediate concerns of Palestinian citizens of Israel. The arithmetic still looks secondary. What Abbas is trying to change is the political value of the seats he expects to win.

Since breaking with the Joint List and entering the Bennett-Lapid coalition in 2021, Abbas has pursued a fairly consistent experiment. His argument, sometimes stated directly and sometimes only through practice, is that Palestinian citizens of Israel have accumulated representation without converting enough of it into governing power.

Arab parties could win ten, thirteen or fifteen seats and still be treated as politically untouchable when coalitions were formed. He tried to break that wall by making Raam available for coalition politics, including with parties whose positions on the Palestinian question were very far from his own. For a short period it worked, then it didn’t.

The government collapsed, Benjamin Netanyahu returned to power, October 7 arrived and the war that followed eroded the legitimacy Abbas had labouriously built for Arab participation in a governing coalition. Jewish opposition parties that desperately need Arab seats to reach a majority still hesitate to say openly that they would govern with Raam. Avigdor Liberman, who sat in the same government with Abbas in 2021, has already said Raam cannot be a coalition partner this time. Netanyahu has gone back to one of his most effective electoral weapons: warning Jewish voters that his opponents will depend on Arab parties to govern.

Segalovich’s place as number two on the list answers that problem more than it answers a shortage of ballots, because the obstacle facing Abbas was never only how many seats Raam might win, but whether those seats would be treated as usable once the counting was over. Jewish opposition parties may need Arab mandates and still refuse to say, in public, that they would govern with them; Netanyahu’s campaign has long fed on that hesitation and Liberman’s rejection of Raam as a partner shows how quickly the old taboo returned after October 7.

A Zionist former police commander standing immediately behind Abbas does not dissolve the ideological objections to the party, yet it makes the simpler charge – that Raam stands outside legitimate Israeli politics – harder to repeat without looking past the man placed in the second slot. He is not only a candidate. He is a certificate of political usability, a way of saying that Arab votes already cast should count towards government rather than remain representation without power. That may be worth more to Abbas after October 7 than the number of Jewish voters Segalovich can actually persuade to put a Raam ballot in the box.

Abbas has again resisted returning to a full Arab Joint List for the same reason. Hadash, Taal and Balad have rebuilt a reduced version of that alliance and left the door open to Raam, but the two projects are no longer travelling in the same direction. The Joint List is trying to maximise collective Arab representation and keep a recognisably Palestinian political address. Abbas is trying to maximise the ability of Arab representation to enter the machinery of government. The aims can overlap. They are not the same. The Joint List has already criticised him for choosing Segalovich rather than rejoining the Arab alliance, and reports before the announcement indicated it was willing to press Raam to return – without Segalovich.

Palestinian politics inside Israel has carried this tension for a long time, longer than one campaign cycle. Should an Arab party first represent the collective political identity of Palestinian citizens, even at the price of remaining outside government? Or should it accept ideological compromise, perhaps a great deal of it, in order to gain access to budgets, ministries and actual decision-making? Abbas has chosen the second route more clearly than any major Arab leader before him. Segalovich takes the experiment one step further. Until now, Abbas argued that an Arab party could cooperate with Zionist parties. He is now saying, in effect, that a Zionist politician can sit inside an Arab-led parliamentary list without either side pretending their ideological differences have disappeared.

Israeli politics has spent decades demanding that Arab politicians prove they are acceptable partners while rarely making the opposite demand of Jewish parties: that they demonstrate a willingness to share political space with Palestinian citizens as equals. Putting Segalovich second on Raam’s list turns that equation around, at least symbolically. The Jewish partner is no longer inviting the Arab into his coalition. He is entering an Arab-led list.

The price is harder to ignore. The more Raam defines its success through its acceptability to Zionist coalition partners, the greater the temptation to push the Palestinian national question further outside its political programme. Segalovich has been explicit that he remains Zionist and Jewish in his political worldview.

Raam has been equally explicit that it is not asking him to become something else. The honesty is better than a fake ideological unity, but it also lays the bargain out in the open. Abbas gains a partner who can help normalise Raam inside Israeli coalition politics. Segalovich joins a slate led by a party whose strategy increasingly emphasises civil integration, crime, budgets and practical governance while leaving the deepest questions of Palestinian national rights somewhere more distant.

The move will not look the same to every part of the electorate. To some Palestinian voters it may demonstrate maturity: politics is about delivering results, not guarding ideological purity from the opposition benches. To others it will look like another stage in transforming Palestinian political power into a tool whose value is measured by how little discomfort it causes the Zionist mainstream. Neither reading is empty. Asking whether Segalovich will bring Raam another seat or two is therefore a smaller question than the one Abbas is actually placing on the table.

He wants the argument after the election to be less about whether Jewish parties are allowed to rely on Arab votes and more about what they are prepared to offer for them. Segalovich is there to make that conversation easier for Jewish politicians. Whether the same move makes Abbas’s argument easier to defend among Palestinian citizens is a separate problem, and he knows it.

That is not simply coexistence. It is a political transaction, and perhaps a very calculated one. The test will not be how many Jewish voters follow Segalovich into Raam on election day. It will come afterwards, when Jewish opposition leaders still have to decide whether they can say publicly what they struggle to say now: that a government supported by Palestinian citizens and their political representatives is no less legitimate because of it.

If Abbas succeeds at that, Segalovich may bring Raam very few additional votes and still prove one of its most consequential candidates. The thing Abbas is really trying to increase is not Raam’s vote share. It is the political worth of an Arab vote after it has already been cast.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: Multipolarity gives middle powers more choices, but fewer guarantees
editorials.passage:
At the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek this week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian received precisely the kind of political support he had hoped for. The SCO condemned the military attacks against Iran, described them as violations of international law and the UN Charter, reaffirmed Iranian sovereignty and territorial integrity, and called for the conflict to be resolved through political and diplomatic means.

But the organisation did not offer to defend Iran. That distinction between political solidarity and collective defence is important. It tells us something not only about the Iranian experience with the SCO, but about the international order that is emerging around it.

For years, discussions about multipolarity have often suggested that the US-led international system would gradually be challenged by an alternative bloc centred around China, Russia and organisations such as BRICS and the SCO. From the perspective of middle powers, joining both institutions seemed to fit neatly into this transformation. Integration into non-Western organisations was supposed to make them less vulnerable to Western isolation and pressure.

The US-Israeli war on Iran has made clear that none of these alternative relationships can produce a security guarantee comparable to those provided by formal military alliances. The lesson is not that multipolarity has failed middle powers. It is that the emerging multipolar order may work differently from what many expected.

Rather than replacing one alliance system with another, it is producing an increasingly dense network of overlapping partnerships in which states gain diplomatic and economic options without necessarily acquiring new security guarantees.

For middle powers, this may be one of the defining characteristics of the emerging order: more room for manoeuvre, but less certainty about who will stand beside them when their security is threatened.

Turkiye provides a particularly revealing example. It has been a member of NATO for more than seven decades and remains embedded in the Western security architecture. Yet Ankara has increasingly demonstrated that alliance membership does not require automatic political alignment with Washington. Turkiye has maintained relations with Russia despite the war in Ukraine, expanded its engagement with China and participated in the SCO as a dialogue partner. At the same time, its differences with the US and Israel over the future regional order in the Middle East have become increasingly visible.

This does not mean Turkiye is abandoning NATO or moving into a Chinese- or Russian-led bloc. Quite the opposite. Ankara’s strategy depends precisely on avoiding such a binary choice. Its NATO membership provides security benefits that the SCO could not replicate. Its relationships with Russia, China, Iran, the Gulf states and other regional actors, meanwhile, expand its diplomatic and economic options.

Brazil represents another good example. Unlike Turkiye, Brazil is not bound to the US through a formal military alliance. But it has traditionally operated within a US-dominated hemisphere where Washington has expected considerable political alignment from regional governments.

Brazil’s refusal to join the US-led Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition (ACCC), together with its positions on the Iran war and other recent international crises, reflects its reluctance to accept that regional proximity should translate into automatic strategic alignment.

Yet Brazil is not simply switching sides. Its participation in BRICS, its extensive economic relationship with China and its calls for reform of the international system coexist with important political and economic relations with the US and Europe. Brasília’s objective is not to exchange dependence on Washington for dependence on Beijing, but to preserve the ability to cooperate with both, and disagree with either.

This may be one of the most consequential opportunities that multipolarity offers middle powers. The rise of alternative centres of economic and political influence reduces the cost of saying no. For decades, weaker states often confronted a difficult choice when facing pressure from a dominant power: comply, resist and risk isolation, or seek protection from a rival bloc.

The proliferation of partners and institutions complicates that calculation. A government that disagrees with Washington may deepen relations with Beijing without becoming a Chinese ally. A state dependent on China economically may strengthen security ties with the US without fully aligning with Washington. Membership in BRICS does not prevent cooperation with Western institutions, just as membership in a US-led security framework does not necessarily preclude engagement with China or Russia.

India has made this logic almost an organising principle of its foreign policy. New Delhi participates in the Quad with the US, Japan and Australia while simultaneously belonging to both BRICS and the SCO. At Bishkek, India supported the SCO declaration defending Iranian sovereignty while Prime Minister Narendra Modi also stressed to Pezeshkian the importance of preserving freedom of navigation and commerce through the Strait of Hormuz.

The Gulf Cooperation Council member states are pursuing their own version of this diversification. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, for example, continue to depend heavily on their relationships with the US for security, while simultaneously expanding economic and diplomatic ties with China, India and other Asian powers and participating in new regional and international arrangements.

None appears eager to replace Washington with Beijing. They want relationships with both. This suggests that the most significant consequence of multipolarity for middle and smaller powers may not be the emergence of a new bloc to which they can attach themselves. It may be the declining necessity of attaching themselves exclusively to any bloc at all.

But greater autonomy comes with a cost. The same flexible arrangements that allow states to avoid choosing sides also provide fewer guarantees when crises become existential. BRICS does not have an Article 5. Neither does the SCO, which explicitly defines itself as a non-military organisation.

Strategic partnerships can provide weapons, investment, diplomatic backing and political support without obligating partners to go to war for one another.

The emerging international system is therefore unlikely to resemble a simple transition from a US-led order to a Chinese-led one, or even a confrontation between two clearly defined blocs. The older alliance system is not disappearing.

NATO remains central to European and Turkish security, while US security relationships remain indispensable across much of Asia and the Gulf. What is emerging alongside it is another layer, a more fluid landscape of overlapping institutions, selective partnerships and transactional relationships.

Multipolarity, in other words, may not require states to choose a new camp. That gives middle and smaller powers greater agency. But it also places greater responsibility for their own security upon them. The world they are entering may offer more partners, more bargaining power and more freedom to say no. What it may offer less frequently is certainty about who will say yes when they ask for protection.

editorials.title: Our pay is called a ‘salary’, but were Roman soldiers really paid in salt?
editorials.passage:
Every second Wednesday, like clockwork, my salary arrives in my bank account. By Thursday, most of it is gone.

Recently, though, as I contemplated its fortnightly appearance and disappearance, I started thinking about the origin of the word “salary”. As a historian of the ancient Roman Empire, I often think about the modern legacy it continues to bestow.

It’s a common belief that the English word “salary” derives from the Latin word salarium because Roman soldiers were sometimes paid in actual blocks of salt.

Sal , the Latin word for salt, also turns up in various other salt-related words in English, from saline to salami .

While it’s an attractively neat idea, there are some significant problems with this theory. Here’s what we actually know about how Roman soldiers were paid.

There’s strong evidence salt was a valuable and widely used commodity in the ancient world. For a society without modern refrigeration, it played an important role in food preservation (particularly for meat and fish). It was also portable, so it’s not surprising that the idea of soldiers being paid in salt caught on.

Peter Gainsford, a New Zealand-based classicist, points out the English word “salary” does indeed derive from the Latin “salarium”, which translates to “stipend or money allowance”.

But, Gainsford argues , while there is a link between “salarium” and “sal”, the Latin word for salt, there is no evidence this link is because Roman soldiers were paid in salt.

The evidence we have suggests Roman soldiers were paid principally in coins, especially silver coins. Roman silver coins often contained images with military themes.

Coins depicting Fides , goddess of good faith and mutual trust, and the term fides militum , meaning “loyalty of the soldiers”, were among the most common .

The ancient Roman historian Livy claimed the Roman state took responsibility for the regular pay of soldiers in 405 BCE. Livy doesn’t tell us the amount, just that they were now paid by the state.

This payment was called the stipendium – from which the modern word “stipend” derives. Up to this point, soldiers had served at their own expense.

Payment of the stipendium was made in instalments three times a year. Deductions were made for clothing, food and even funeral provisions before the net amount was paid to soldiers.

More than three centuries later, in around 50 BCE, Julius Caesar doubled the stipendium to 225 denarii per year. A loaf of bread at the time cost up to a quarter of one denarius.

By the end of the second century CE, the amount had increased to 600 denarii. Note, these were the figures for ordinary foot soldiers or legionaries. Centurions and other officers were paid at considerably higher rates.

Over time, however, the stipendium was not enough. Problems with inflation, especially in the third century CE, led to soldiers demanding greater pay.

Supplemental payments were made to soldiers, especially in a form called donativa which were essentially a kind of bonus. These bonuses significantly increased the total income they received.

Donativa were paid annually and bound the army’s loyalty more directly to individual emperors. Emperors understood that paying donativa at lower amounts or refusing to pay them altogether potentially caused disloyalty.

As the emperor Septimius Severus (reigned 193–211 CE) lay on his deathbed, advice he gave to his sons demonstrated the importance of this idea clearly: “Be harmonious, enrich the soldiers, and scorn all other men.”

Once a Roman soldier swore the military oath, known as the sacramentum , it was typically expected he would give 25 years of service.

However, regular income – together with the possibility of bonuses – made serving in the army an attractive proposition for many. There were other benefits for soldiers, too.

On their retirement, soldiers received the praemia militiae , a lump sum of 3,000 denarii (12,000 sesterces) at the time of Augustus’ reign towards the end of the first century BCE. This increased over time.

In the fourth century CE (and perhaps earlier), soldiers also received an allowance for food, clothing and other items. This was raised from a special tax called the annona militaris .

A crisis in the silver currency in the third century saw soldiers lose faith in its value .

In the fourth century, during the reign of the emperor Constantine (306–337), a new gold piece was minted . This was known as the solidus .

The solidus weighed 4.5 grams, replacing the earlier aureus of 7.5 grams. It became the most trusted and reliable denomination in the Roman world for a thousand years.

Soldiers were its key beneficiary and there is a popular suggestion that the word “soldier” derives from solidus .

However, similar to suggestions of the origins of “salary” and salt, there is no clear evidence that “soldier” derives from solidus.

Read more: This history of currencies suggests the US dollar’s dominance may fade – but it will happen slowly

Thousands of words in modern English and European languages have their origins in Latin (and also ancient Greek). The connection between “salary” and the Latin word salarium is an example.

The preservation qualities of salt made it a vital commodity for soldiers. On campaign and in barracks it was a necessity.

There is no evidence, however, that this was connected to Roman soldiers being paid in salt. Coins did that job admirably.

editorials.title: Ramachandra Guha: For 120 years, Indian students have fought to change politics and public life
editorials.passage:
In early July, as the students’ protests in Jantar Mantar were taking shape, the Trinamool Congress MP, Mahua Moitra, was one of the first politicians to show up in person and offer solidarity. Three weeks later, when the Union education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, resigned, Moitra thanked the younger generation “for saving Indian democracy” by bringing “this fascist, arrogant government to its knees”.

This, as she pointed out, was something the Opposition parties had not been able to do in the past 12 years.

Mahua Moitra’s praise was well merited. The resignation of the education minister, the home minister’s prolonged absence from Parliament, the sacking of several senior BJP office-bearers, and – not least – the clumsy, late-night videos of the prime minister, all testified to a regime whose customary air of hubristic arrogance had (at least temporarily) given way to weakness and confusion

It is too early to say whether the momentum that the student “cockroaches” have thus far generated can be sustained, leading to a fuller renewal of the constitutional promises of liberty, equality and fraternity. Historians are not astrologers, so, instead of projecting forward, I shall here look backwards, exploring other times in the past when Indian students have sought to leave their impress on politics and public life.

The first such occasion was 120 years ago, during the swadeshi movement in Bengal. As Sumit Sarkar observed in his book on that particular upsurge, “Students of every district came to study in Calcutta, and no doubt it was through them above all that the movement initially spread into the mofussil.” While the more prominent leaders came from the established professional and landed classes, writes Sarkar, “the volunteers themselves of course came largely from the student community, many of them of extremely tender years”.

In subsequent years, students energetically participated in the movements against British colonial rule led by Mahatma Gandhi and the Indian National Congress. Male students joined the Non-co-operation and Civil Disobedience movements in large numbers, organising demonstrations and courting arrest. Students were even more active in the Quit India movement, filling the jails in their thousands.

A feature of Quit India was the dynamic role played by young women. The stirring story of Usha Mehta, the Bombay University student who helped organise the underground “Congress radio”, has been documented in an excellent book by Usha Thakkar.

But there were other notable (if now less known) examples too. A file I found in the archives, titled “Karnatak in Revolt”, narrates how the “most phenomenal feature” of the movement in this part of India was the response of the student community, which organised boycotts and hartals in Belgaum, Gadag, Bangalore, Mysore, Mangalore, Bijapur, Bellari, Sirsi and other places.

On October 23, 1942, two students from Dharwad, a Miss Shenolikar and a Miss Gulawadi, entered the district court, hoisted the national flag, told the district judge (who was present) that he was dismissed from his office, distributed leaflets, and disappeared. (There the archival trail runs out – one would love to know what happened to Miss Shenolikar and Miss Gulawadi in later life.)

In the decades leading up to Independence, students were active in social and political movements. What of the years after India rid itself of colonial rule? In 1968, the American scholar, Philip G. Altbach, edited a book titled Turmoil and Transition: Higher Education and Student Politics in India . In his introduction, Altbach remarked that while “students played a key role in the struggle of Independence”, since 1947 “most student agitation has not been directly political, but has concerned non-ideological issues”.

The book’s case studies examined the “non-ideological issues” raised by students in the 1960s which included not only high fees and poor hostel facilities but also cultural activities such as music and theatre.

Within a year of this book’s publication, students had re-entered politics, playing a major role in the movement for a separate state of Telangana which started in 1969, although it bore final fruition long afterwards. This was one of three regional movements in post-Independence India that have strongly featured students. The others were the Assam movement of the late 1970s/early 1980s and the Uttarakhand movement of the 2000s.

Of the Assam agitation, the historian, Arupjyoti Saikia, writes that “the movement was largely in the hands of student leaders”, whose “idealism inspired large numbers; when they delivered their fiery speeches, crowds of both women and men listened in rapt attention”. The All Assam Students’ Union gave birth to the Asom Gana Parishad, which won an assembly election in 1985. Three decades later, students also helped propel the Telangana Rashtra Samithi to power in that state.

All these struggles form the unacknowledged prehistory of the movement currently underway. However, the most obvious precursor from the past is the “JP movement” of the mid 1970s in which students played such a prominent part. In his book, Protest Movements in Two Indian States , Ghanshyam Shah carefully documents the course of the protests in Gujarat and Bihar.

In both states, students played a leading role. In Gujarat, the Congress chief minister, Chimanbhai Patel, was widely seen as corrupt, becoming a prime target of youth anger. Students attacked the then prime minister, Indira Gandhi, for protecting Chimanbhai and for not being able to stem price rise. The protests were by no means non-violent, featuring attacks on government property and the looting of shops.

Shah writes that, as in Gujarat, “students were the vanguard of the Bihar movement” of the 1970s. However, unlike in Gujarat, in Bihar one elderly individual played a key leadership role. This was Jayaprakash Narayan. As Shah observes, “his concern for the poor, his moral stance, his simplicity and humility”, all contributed to the veteran freedom-fighter’s charisma. JP appealed to the students to give up studies for a year to “save democracy”.

The students who flocked to his call included members of the right-wing Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad and also many young socialist activists.

The present student upsurge resembles the JP movement in one significant manner. The principal targets of both have been authoritarianism and the cult of personality, as represented in the 1970s by Indira Gandhi and her party and by Narendra Modi and his party now. Yet there are also major differences. The ABVP was then against the ruling regime; now it is firmly on the side of the ruling regime. It does also seem that, compared to the JP movement, women students are more visible in the current protests, their idealism and courage reminiscent of the female satyagrahis of 1942.

The upsurge of the 1970s presented itself as a second freedom struggle, working to finally fulfil the failed promises of the first. In so far as it helped end one-party rule and brought about a fresh wind of democracy, the movement succeeded. On the other hand, the JP movement also gave legitimacy to the forces of Hindutva, which have steadily gathered power and influence in the years that followed.

To their credit, the student leaders of the present resolutely oppose both authoritarianism and religious bigotry.

The invocation by them of Ambedkar, Gandhi and Nehru – all together – suggests that they see their movement as a third freedom struggle, working to finally fulfil the failed promises of the first and the second. How far these ideals will be realised in the years ahead shall depend on the actions of countless individuals and organisations, many of whom who were not themselves present in Jantar Mantar during those heady days of June and July.

This article first appeared in The Telegraph.

editorials.title: Have attacks on ‘Anandabazar Patrika’ proven its ‘saffron hooliganism’ headline right?
editorials.passage:
Days after West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari demanded an apology from Anandabazar Patrika for using the term “saffron hooliganism” in a headline, a mob arrived at the newspaper’s Kolkata office on September 1 to prove that the newspaper was right.

The mob, which included members of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party , smeared the publication’s compound wall with saffron paint on Tuesday. They shouted slogans criticising the Bengali daily, one of the oldest newspapers in the country, chanting “bhagwa ka apman nahi sahega Hindustan”. India will not tolerate insults to saffron.

Saffron is the sacred colour of Hinduism but has been adopted by the BJP as its signature hue.

The Bengali daily had used the phrase “gerua gundami”, or saffron hooliganism, to describe the August 20 violence at Jadavpur University. That day, members of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad, the student wing of BJP’s ideological parent the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, had clashed with Left-affiliated student groups on campus.

“The people who entered the campus of Jadavpur University and did hooliganism – they demeaned saffron, not us,” said a journalist working at the newspaper, requesting anonymity.

The journalist added: “We vividly described whatever happened that day along with photographs. Everything – the article and the photograph – substantiated the headline.”

The journalist has worked at Anandabazar Patrika for decades. He said that the paper, the most-read daily in Bengal, had weathered hostility from previous governments of the Left Front, the Trinamool and the Congress. “For a short while, advertisements were stopped,” he said. “But never did an outfit attack the main building. Nobody did that.”

Videos uploaded by BJP members on Facebook show police personnel standing around as men wearing saffron painted the pillars of the compound. “The police remained mute spectators,” the journalist said.

On August 28, the police had registered a first information report against staffers of the newspapers. Hours later, Chief Minister Adhikari followed up with a warning that anyone seen to be attacking saffron will “not be able to handle the terrible consequences”.

The next day, the journalist said, he saw a group of eight to 10 persons protesting outside the newspaper office. “I was coming in and going out of the office for some errand,” he said. “I saw them raising slogans against Anandabazar Patrika, mostly in Hindi.” The same slogans were shouted again on September 1, but this time the mob was bigger, he noted.

He said if somebody had an objection to the headline, there were democratic ways of protesting. “One can write a letter to the editor, and generally those letters are also published with due respect,” he said.

But, in this case, he noted: “The chief minister himself incited people.”

The journalist added: “The dangerous element with this government is that if you oppose them, if they don’t like anything your writing, they brand you as anti-nationals.”

The same thing has happened to the students of Jadavpur University, he continued. “Whatever slogans they are writing, you may not like them, but you can’t call them anti-national for that,” he said.

The protesters asked the newspaper to apologise but the ABP Group, the parent organisation of the Anandabazar Patrika , did not succumb to that pressure, the journalist said.

“So whatever they’re trying to do, they’re trying to make us frightened,” he said. “They want us to cower down to their pressure.”

He said that the intimidation had left an impact on the newsroom. “We feel insecure,” he said. “We feel concerned. We feel anxious for the safety of our colleagues.”

While the staff were determined to continue their work despite the threats, he said that they “cannot wait for something more grave to happen”.

Even as many media organisations protested this incident, the Press Club in Calcutta had been silent, the journalist pointed out. “This issue is not only about a particular newspaper, it’s about the freedom of press,” he said.

The journalist added: “Everybody wants a free working atmosphere. We don’t want to become heroes. Fighting the government or a very influential political party is not our job. We are here to report facts.”

Here is a summary of last week’s top stories.

Voting rights. The names of more than two crore persons were removed from Maharashtra’s draft voter list as part of the special intensive revision of electoral rolls. The excluded electors account for 21.1% of the state’s previous voter base.

In Delhi, 47.7 lakh names were deleted from the draft list. They account for 33% of the Union Territory’s electorate.

Those removed from the voter list were marked as either permanently shifted, deceased, absent, duplicate entries or placed under the “other” category, which includes those who refused to fill the enumeration form.

Voters can file claims and objections against their exclusion from the draft list between August 31 and September 30. The appeals will be heard by October 29. The final electoral roll will be published on November 4.

More than six crore names have been deleted from draft lists of several states during the ongoing phase of the exercise.

Scroll’s SIR experience is a microcosm of what urban India is facing

Ex-bureaucrat booked for a tweet. Former civil servant Ashish Joshi, who was picked up during his morning walk on Wednesday by plainclothes police personnel and interrogated for several hours, said on Friday that a first information report had been registered against him for a social media post. It was filed under sections pertaining to provocation with the intent to cause a riot.

The FIR was registered for a post he made on August 26, in which he had reportedly called for a “Nuremberg-style trial” of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Joshi, however, said that he had been questioned about another post from last month, in which he had alleged that there had been a “massive showdown” between Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Home Secretary Govind Mohan after the police action against students protesting at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.

NSA detention quashed. The Allahabad High Court quashed the preventive detention of 25-year-old Aakriti Chaudhary under the National Security Act. The Delhi University graduate has been in jail for nearly five months in connection with the workers’ protest in Noida.

The court held that she was detained by the Uttar Pradesh government based on a “concocted story”. The Noida authorities were directed to pay Chaudhary Rs 5 lakh as compensation.

However, she will remain in jail as she is yet to secure bail in other cases registered in connection with the April protests.

editorials.title: September Indian fiction: Six new titles (including Amit Chaudhuri’s) to look forward to
editorials.passage:
All information sourced from publishers.

A writer is invited to Paris and finds himself living in an area that bears little resemblance to his idea of the city. With the passing of time, his disquiet translates into a way of seeking and experiencing a truer, more unlikely Paris.

Château Rouge takes up residence in that area before floating freely through the city. It takes its time, exploring tangents, diversions, side streets, creeping into new spaces and remote angles, to open up fresh ground and appraise the city, the experience of travel, otherness – and the novel itself – anew.

It is 1916, and the First World War is raging across Europe. Madhusudan Chandra Joshi is a young Indian clerk working at the District Courts when he travels to Heidelberg to study law. There, a chance encounter with the mysterious revolutionary Amir Farooqui changes the course of his life.

Drawn into the secretive Hindu–German Conspiracy, a revolutionary gun-running plot organised by Indians living in exile, Madhusudan finds himself caught up in a dangerous international struggle for Indian independence from British colonial rule. As the conspiracy unfolds across India, Europe and America, the outbreak of war makes it increasingly impossible for Madhusudan and Amir to remain in Heidelberg.

Madhusudan travels to London, determined to continue his legal studies, while Amir heads to San Francisco in search of fellow revolutionaries. But London exposes Madhusudan to the harsh realities of British colonialism, racism and inequality. Far from home and caught between his ambitions and his growing political awareness, he must confront truths he can no longer escape.

A glamorous address, an immaculate home, a seemingly perfect family – Radhika Khanna appears to glide through Delhi society.

Yet before dawn she is already on edge, coaxing her hair into place, weighing herself with dread, rehearsing the smile that keeps awkward questions at bay.

When a confrontation at her daughter’s elite school turns Radhika from admired committee head to whispered cautionary tale, fissures spread through her meticulously managed world: fragile neighbourhood-mom alliances, an uneasy bond with her yoga teacher-friend and the carefully curated social media posts that mask an unbearable loneliness. As gala weekends and themed dinners hurtle towards a spectacular destination party in Rajasthan, Radhika is forced to pay the true price of her perfection.

When the Emergency descends upon India in 1975, Srinivasa Rao is an ordinary Telugu lecturer in an ordinary college in Andhra Pradesh, whose greatest loyalties are to his family and the routines of everyday life. While he loves Telugu literature, he keeps a distance from revolutionary and progressive writers’ organisations and has never considered himself a political activist. Yet one midnight in 1976, the police arrive at his door, and he is taken to a detention camp without explanation. Why was he arrested and detained? Is it a story he wrote long ago? Is it his friendships? Is it his occasional attendance at progressive literary gatherings? Is it his signature on a petition against the college management protesting unfair conditions? The reasons remain inscrutable to the end.

Over 19 harrowing nights, Srinivasa Rao secretly records his thoughts on smuggled scraps of paper, under stolen shards of light, creating an intimate diary of fear, uncertainty and endurance. As he witnesses arbitrary arrests, interrogation, humiliation and the devastation wrought by unchecked state power, he is forced to confront unsettling questions about justice, freedom and the cost of remaining silent.

Meet a demon who comforts its victim before possessing her, a live-in maid plotting quiet revenge, and a sceptic who falls in love with a spirit he set out to disprove.

In Peace in the Land of the Dead , Lian Dousel’s debut collection, 12 stories carry readers to Manipur, where reality is blurred, heightened and transformed by the surreal. Our protagonists encounter demons that decide their fate and hear laments of sentient woodlands, wonder “what if” and find out too late, and confront us with the fragility and endurance of human life.

First published in 1955, Wandered the Traveller is a lost classic of South Asian literature – now available in English for the first time in Daisy Rockwell’s translation.

Nisar Aziz Butt’s semi-autobiographical novel follows Afgar, a brilliant young Pashtun woman, from a turbulent orphaned childhood, through the cloistered world of a mountain sanatorium, to the brink of departure in pursuit of a doctorate at Cambridge. Fiercely intelligent yet yearning for love, Afgar measures each man she meets against the standards of her own restless mind, and finds them wanting.

editorials.title: ‘The Grave Exhumers and Other Stories’: A close-up of Muslim lives outside Kolkata’s urban premises
editorials.passage:
The stories in The Grave Exhumers and Other Stories by Lutfor Rahaman were written when he was 21 years old. To be 21 and have such a deep-rooted grasp of the colour, habitation, geography, and taste of the air is remarkable to witness. And what’s more impressive is the fact that translator Mursed Alam has managed to get these details and idiosyncrasies without diluting them.

Comprising six short stories, the collection zeroes down on death in some or the other form. For instance, even a seemingly optimistic story (at least by the title) called “Collectors of Hope” , starts thus: “Sohrab lost the job, finally!”

Death looms over the reader like a crow perched on an ever-drying branch. Through death, Rahaman manages to construct a world on the margins, all set in a village on the outskirts of Kolkata. The stories become important because they provide a foil to the canonical Bengali literature – the Tagores and the Chattopadhyays – and take us down to the cellular level of the lives of Muslim communities in rural areas.

Reading Rahaman’s world is like stepping into something new. His protagonists, who are mostly poor Muslim inhabitants, are always facing some or another obstacle. And, while you’re reading, you might think that these inhabitants would leverage some sort of morality against survival, but they don’t. Their goal is to get through the day without intellectualising their struggle. Rahaman steers clear of it as well – he refuses to let the audience pity his characters. Instead, he invites us in, piques our curiosity, and makes us embarrassed to be voyeurs.

Each story also uses nature for this effect. For instance: “The sky is pitch-black. The wind cloud rinsed the soul of the whole world before thickly blanketing it. The moon is nowhere to be found. It might have died.”

The characters are gritty, resilient, and religious – the last one being the driving force behind many of the decisions that they make. However, something trumps this ferventness as well – the desire to live a decent life; to separate themselves from the animals they tend. Dignity is elusive; it comes and goes and is subject to many conditions. This is illustrated by these lines: The grave or hell are all owned by those mollahs. Our hungry belly is our Allah, understood?”

Nature and its hellish crusades are prominent themes in these stories. The rain is shown to ravage the fields, crops, and houses. Everything is tinged with greys, blacks, and blues and painted with a brush of destruction. The characters are at the mercy of an inhospitable nature; this might explain why they’re resilient – they have no other option but to be that way. This gives the stories a Sisyphian colour – it seems like one story has been reincarnated six times.

The destructive side of nature is translated with economy and alignment in the author’s voice, which in turn is recreated in English by Mursed Alam. Here’s one of my favourite lines to supplement my bubbling praise: “The graveyard-night had strangled the pregnant moon a while back.”

Alam’s translation brings Rahaman’s world alive and prods the reader to empathise with its protagonists, who are labourers, farmers, and daily wage earners, but without a patronising gaze.

With these six stories, both the author and the translator take us on a journey across borders and beyond the usual Bengali translations that we’ve engaged with. By retaining the visual finesse of the source text, Alam manages to translate the voices on the margins that Rahaman first put in the spotlight.

The Grave Exhumers and Other Stories, Lutfor Rahaman, translated from the Bengali by Mursed Alam, Yoda Press.

editorials.title: Indo-Pacific’s future runs through the Indian Ocean
editorials.passage:
Tumultuous changes have been occurring in global geopolitics over the last couple of years. These include the onset of pandemics, war in the Eurasian heartland and complex US-China ties, which are defining the contours of global geopolitics.

In addition, supply chain disruptions, conflicts in maritime corridors, and the weaponisation of critical mineral trading are also new forms of geopolitical complexity affecting the global order. According to UNCTAD statistics from April 2025, “Maritime transport moves over 80 per cent of goods traded worldwide”. The onset of the Iran-US war and the subsequent Hormuz crisis have had a major impact on maritime trade.

It is in this framework that one can envisage the importance of the Indian Ocean in shaping the geopolitics of the Indo-Pacific. Ever since Donald Trump began his second term in office and upended US engagement in West Asia, newer security challenges have come up in the Indo-Pacific region as well. Despite the somewhat changing position of the US, the Indo-Pacific security structure remains important in the global security structure. The Indian Ocean too remains critical to the overall global maritime security structure. From an Indian perspective, the Indian Ocean provides an anchor point through which it can effectively navigate the evolving geopolitics in both the IOR and the broader Indo-Pacific matrix.
Mapping the Indian Ocean to the Indo-Pacific Structure
Over the years, the Indian Ocean has provided the necessary impetus to global trade and commerce. This region is endowed with natural resources, including critical minerals and conventional energy sources such as oil and gas. There exists significant potential for the blue economy in the Indian Ocean region as well.

Major geopolitical flashpoints like the Russia-Ukraine war, the Red Sea crisis, the current geopolitical quagmire in West Asia and tensions in the South China Sea are occurring in the Indian Ocean region and around it.

One of the most important security challenges that both the Indian Ocean and the Pacific Ocean are currently grappling with is the rise of China and the security challenges it is posing to both the Indian Ocean littoral states and the Pacific. China has launched an ambitious plan to control the sea lanes and to station its marine command unit at one of the key entry points of the Indian Ocean. Similarly, its naval bases in Gwadar and control over Hambantota are going to pose a subtle challenge to the maritime security of the Indian Ocean.
Challenges for Indo-Pacific
In recent years, the US, which is an Indo-Pacific power, has taken a back seat in this regard. This is evident from the fact that, in June 2026, the name of the US Indo-Pacific Command was reverted to US Pacific Command, which was created in 1947. By changing the name, what the United States is signalling requires closer analysis. Though the United States justified the name change as a tribute to its war heroes, the strategic implications, as reported, are manifold.

When the US took a decision to rename the Indo-Pacific Command as Pacific Command, the US and China rebooted their relationship and took it to new heights. Moreover, President Donald Trump visited China in May 2026 and expanded the scope of transactional relations between the two. It may be added that even before Trump’s visit, the US Administration was mulling over improving its economic relations with China.

Significantly, the US National Security Strategy 2025 emphasises improving economic ties with China. At the same time, China’s desire to improve ties with the US is evident in its somewhat neutral stance during the ongoing war between the US and Iran. This is even though China and Iran have a strong bilateral relationship. It has also been argued that, following his visit to China in May 2026, the Trump Administration is adopting a cautious stance on the Taiwan Strait without diluting the US’s original position on the Taiwan question. Keeping all the above strategic considerations in mind, it is pertinent to highlight how India needs to look at the changing geopolitical realignment in the Indo-Pacific.
India’s Strategic Engagement with Indo-Pacific
Over time, India has approached the Indo-Pacific region as one of the strategic pillars of its foreign policy. As the pivotal player in the Indian Ocean Region, India plays an important role in shaping the region’s geopolitics. One may add here that Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s speech in Mauritius in 2015 outlined India’s strategic doctrine, SAGAR (Sustainable Growth for All in the Region), which underlines the need for sustainable security in the Indian Ocean Region and highlights the paramount role of India in this region. Prior to the SAGAR doctrine, some strategies, such as the Look East and Act East policies, were already in place. Both Look East and Act East policies recognise the “centrality” of ASEAN.

Another important milestone in the evolution of Indo-Pacific strategy was the “US-India Joint Strategic Vision for the Asia-Pacific and Indian Ocean Region” signed in 2015 by India and the US. According to this Strategic Vision, “India and the United States are important drivers of regional and global growth. From Africa to East Asia, we will build on our partnership to support sustainable, inclusive development, and increased regional connectivity”. This Strategic Vision has also paved the way for underpinning the broader geopolitical notion of “Indo-Pacific”.

It was in 2021 that the first online meeting of Quad (India, Australia, Japan, and the US) leaders took place. In the Quad, India plays an important role in shaping the broader canvas for this grouping, spanning climate change, critical technology, and infrastructure development. Now India needs to re-examine its role due to major geopolitical churnings underway at present. This is especially true in the context of a milder shift in US policy towards this geopolitical region.

India’s initiatives to augment its strategic cooperation with Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and Indonesia are a welcome development. Another aspect that needs to be emphasised here is that the visit of the Japanese Premier, Sanae Takaichi, to India in the first week of July marked a new beginning in India’s Indian Ocean and Indo-Pacific strategies. The flurry of geopolitical engagement in and around the Indo-Pacific region by three Quad member countries, along with Indonesia and New Zealand, signals that these countries share common geopolitical and geo-economic dynamism that can sustain the region’s geopolitics. Prime Minister Modi’s visit to these three countries, along with Indonesia and New Zealand, signalled important geopolitical postures of India.

While India remains committed to the idea of Quad, it is also taking important steps towards strategising its cooperation with the member countries on important issues at the bilateral level. Though India and the US share a common strategic posture in the Indo-Pacific region, Washington’s recent strategic move towards greater economic engagement with Beijing certainly generated apprehension in New Delhi. By leveraging its partnerships with Australia, Japan, New Zealand and Indonesia, India can address some of the core bilateral issues like clean energy, technological cooperation, greater economic collaboration, as well as the question of the Open Indo-Pacific, etc. Another important aspect that needs to be highlighted is that Prime Minister Modi started his diplomacy by visiting Indonesia first, which occupies an important position in the Indian Ocean region.

The visit of Prime Minister Modi to Australia, New Zealand and Indonesia reflects India’s Mahasagar initiative. This strategic doctrine of Mahasagar (Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions) was outlined by the Prime Minister during his visit to Mauritius in March 2025. The Mahasagar initiative aims at enhancing and strengthening sustainable security, giving primacy to the Blue Economy, mitigating climatic disasters, and enhancing the construction of ports and connectivity projects. This initiative, also known as the “Great Ocean Initiative,” aims to provide greater leverage to India’s maritime connectivity projects.

The Mahasagar initiative will strengthen India’s geopolitical strategies by countering China’s aggressive naval strategies, such as the BRI and the PLAN, which, over the years, have posed a substantial challenge to peace and security in the Indian Ocean Region and the Indo-Pacific geopolitical construct. At the same time, through port and infrastructure connectivity, India can also augment its presence in Africa. This can improve trade relations with Africa.

Similarly, through this initiative, India can also effectively connect with the small island countries of the Indo-Pacific.

What is needed is an inclusive Indo-Pacific in which geopolitics and geoeconomics can operate within an “equilibrium” framework. India’s Mahasagar doctrine should also embrace the Mediterranean strategic framework, as this is an important sea connecting both the Black Sea and the Red Sea, as well as the Indian Ocean. This geopolitical realignment can be in the framework of the “Greater Indo-Pacific”. There is a need to counter expanding NATO in the Indo-Pacific region.

The interaction among three strategically vital regions of the world throughout history was aptly highlighted by Kalidas Nag in his book The Greater India. Through the Indian Ocean route, India can connect with the emerging Northern Sea Route. It will facilitate India’s entry into the Arctic region. Moreover, through the Indo-Pacific Corridor, India can also reach out to Russia through the Chennai-Vladivostok Maritime Corridor. This, to a great extent, will contribute to augmenting India-Russia trade and economic cooperation. Similarly, through the Altai region, where Russia and Kazakhstan share a border, oil can be transported to India. The same can be done from Kazakhstan through two rivers — Altai and Irtysh — to Russia’s Siberian port Sabetta.

In a nutshell, it can be added that the Indian Ocean helps India shape its maritime as well as continental policy. The same can be inferred from the Great Nicobar Project, which India has enunciated in recent years. The Great Nicobar Project aims to augment India’s presence in the Strait of Malacca while also checkmating China’s belligerent moves.

A closer look at global maritime geopolitics in recent years demonstrates that its importance is increasing day by day. The onset of the Iran-US war and the subsequent Strait of Hormuz crisis demonstrate the importance of chokepoints and maritime connectivity corridors. It is in this context that one can see the importance of the Indian and Pacific Oceans in global geopolitics.

Due to its strategic location, as well as its vast extent, it connects continents of Asia and Africa. Along with the Eastern Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean is going to shape the geopolitical dynamics of the vast tract of landmass. Throughout history, this coastline along the Indian Ocean has played a critical role in geopolitical dynamics. It has been observed that the emergence of the Indo-Pacific has substantially altered the geopolitical landscape. It is in this context that one can see the importance of this geopolitical zone.

Though the US Administration is re-examining the strategic concept, one thing that needs to be underlined here is that it cannot abandon the Indo-Pacific strategic framework. Thus, here lies the importance of the Greater Indo-Pacific, which can bring strategic convergence to the Indo-Pacific. India, as the pivotal player in the Indian Ocean region, can provide the necessary stability to the Indo-Pacific geopolitical structure.

(The author teaches at the School of International Studies, JNU, New Delhi. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: ‘Pakistan is imploding’: Ex-diplomat on Balochistan, Indus Waters and Dhurandhar
editorials.passage:
In an exclusive interview with Firstpost, Rajiv Dogra — former Ambassador to Italy, Romania, Moldova and Albania, and the last Indian Consul General in Karachi — speaks about Pakistan’s never-ending crises, Britain’s role in its creation and its support for Mohammed Ali Jinnah’s Partition plan. He also explains why he believes the Narendra Modi government has rightly suspended the Indus Waters Treaty, recalls the violence he witnessed during his stay in Karachi, weighs in on Dhurandhar’s depiction of Pakistani society, and argues that Islamabad-Rawalpindi is fast losing its grip on Balochistan.

The following is the second and final part of edited excerpts from the interview:

Q: There is a common thread running through almost all your books, from Where Borders Bleed to How Nations Fail. In all your books, you examine diplomacy and geostrategy through historical and civilisational prisms, while also seeking to develop a distinctly Indian perspective. Why?

A: When I started researching my first book, Where Borders Bleed, I found that much of our knowledge and interpretation of history, at least in books, had been shaped by British authors. With some exceptions, many Indian historians also followed the British way of looking at history. Lord Mountbatten, for instance, is famously reported to have said that he did not know Mohammed Ali Jinnah was dying and that, had he known, he would have delayed the announcement of Partition. I found that difficult to accept. Even photographs of Jinnah from the 1930s onwards showed that he was becoming increasingly ill. There was enough other evidence. When he was travelling from Bombay to Lahore for the Lahore Resolution, for example, he had to be taken off the train for medical treatment. He was that ill.

Jinnah had also spent seven years in London, where he consulted doctors. It was not just the two Parsi doctors in Bombay; several doctors knew about his illness. At the time, British intelligence was regarded as the best in the world. It is difficult to imagine that the health of someone as important as Jinnah would not have been known to the British. More strikingly, Lord Wavell, Mountbatten’s predecessor, wrote in his handover note that Jinnah was ill, suffering from tuberculosis and could die at any moment. The British had also decided on Partition soon after the Second World War. I brought these facts out in Where Borders Bleed. For me, there was immense satisfaction in moving away from the British interpretation of history.

The second major change I tried to bring to Foreign Service writing was to move away from memoirs. Most officers before me wrote about their own experiences. In none of my books is there an ‘I’ factor. There are many things I could say about what I have done for India, but I decided my books should not be about me. They should be about my country and its history, and that history should be shared with my fellow citizens. That is why almost every book of mine begins at the very beginning. My latest book, How Nations Fail, too, starts with the beginnings of civilisation. When societies and civilisations emerged, they went through periods of rise and decline. Remarkably, those cycles have followed similar patterns.

What happened to the Indus Valley Civilisation, for example, was linked to shifts in the river system, which forced people to migrate to areas where agriculture was possible. That also contains a lesson for the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty. Today, we must be very careful. If Pakistan gets its way and India is unable to derive the full benefit of its own waters, there will be serious consequences.

In 1960, when the Indus Waters Treaty was signed, Jammu and Kashmir had nearly 700 lakes — 697, to be precise. Seventy-seven per cent of them have either shrunk dramatically or disappeared. We should learn from the Indus civilisation and recognise the considerable damage that, in my view, has already been caused by a flawed Indus Waters Treaty. That is why lessons from the past are so important in understanding the present.

There is also a common theme in the decline of nations: nations begin to decline when their people lose faith in them. Wars and a bad economy matter, but the most important factor is the mindset of the people. If people lose confidence in their nation’s ability to progress, decline begins. Ultimately, it is the will and ambition of a people — and their leaders — that drive a nation.

 

Q: Since you mentioned India’s water security, how should New Delhi approach the issue now? Water is crucial for India, but it is also critical for Pakistan.

A: We have to understand that Pakistan has been spoiled immensely because much of the Indus water flowing through the country is wasted. Nearly 30 to 40 per cent flows into the ocean, whereas India has suffered all along. But the important question is what India should do now. I hope India does not simply say that the Indus Waters Treaty is in abeyance and assume that is the end of the matter. Pakistan is already in overdrive on the issue, just as it was over Kashmir in 1947.

At the time, we hoped our moral position — including going to the UN — would convince the world that we were right and that Pakistan should be driven out of Jammu and Kashmir. That did not happen because the world does not operate purely on morality. It operates on pragmatism. Pakistan is now repeating history. It is going around the world saying, ‘India is depriving us of water.’ India must put forward its case and explain the circumstances surrounding a treaty that was imposed on it.

There is no other example in the world where a treaty between two sovereign nations was effectively imposed through the intervention of a bank. There should be no role for a bank between two sovereign nations. That happened because the Americans wanted it that way. They did not want a direct role, but they were pulling the strings. Jawaharlal Nehru was in a difficult position because of India’s economic circumstances at the time. He also believed the treaty might make Pakistan recognise the value of cooperation. But that proved disastrous. We have paid for it through water scarcity in places such as Jammu and Srinagar. Wular Lake has also shrunk, directly affecting the ecology, tourism and production in the area. Our agricultural and industrial objectives have suffered.

Second, there is no treaty in the world that cannot be revised. Turkey, for example, decided it needed to build more dams and overturned long-standing arrangements with Iraq and Syria. The Euphrates and Tigris no longer flowed into those countries at their previous levels because Turkey was storing water and building dams. In 1960, when the Indus Waters Treaty was being imposed on India, America had also decided that Mexico would not receive its full share of water. We live in a transactional world, and India must be firm about its needs and necessities. We must seriously consider abrogating this treaty, which I believe was unfairly imposed on India.

 

Q: In an earlier conversation with me, you spoke about Dawood Ibrahim. There are reports that he is extremely unwell. The film, Dhurandhar, too, has a scene suggesting that he was poisoned by Indian intelligence. What do you make of that?

A: That might be the case. I do not know whether he was poisoned. But Dhurandhar is 100 per cent correct in its portrayal of the wild and gruesome nature of Pakistani society.

 

Q: You were in Karachi during a period of intense violence and criminal activity. What did you witness?

A: I was there between 1992 and 1994. Muhajirs, Baloch and Pathans were involved in running battles all the time. There were struggles over control of resources, drugs and other criminal activities.

Three days after the 1993 Bombay blasts, I was invited to a dinner in Karachi, where I was posted then. I saw a man sitting in the garden with a couple of Pakistanis. Later I was told he was Tiger Memon. The moment I saw him, he was quickly taken inside. That was the kind of society we were dealing with.

 Rajiv Dogra, former Ambassador to Italy, Romania, Moldova and Albania, and the last Indian Consul General in Karachi, Pakistan, has just written a book, ‘How Nations Fail and the Unmaking of America’s World’. (Photo by Ram Dogra)

Q: How do you see the situation in Balochistan? Has it spiralled beyond Islamabad’s control, or can Pakistan still contain it?

A: It has spiralled out of control for the Pakistani authorities in Balochistan. They essentially control only the urban areas. Even there, the situation is difficult. The problem for the BLA and other groups is numbers. Balochistan has also seen significant Punjabi settlement. The original Baloch population is relatively small compared with the province’s overall population. Geographically, it is Pakistan’s largest province.

Whether the insurgents can sustain their campaign depends on recruitment and the support they receive. If the TTP and BLA become aggressive simultaneously, the difficulties for the Pakistan Army will multiply. The TTP, however, is not as consistent as the BLA in targeting the Pakistan Army.

 

Q: Amid these crises, the improvement in Pakistan-US ties has come as a major relief for Islamabad. Donald Trump appears to have developed a strange rapport with Pakistan’s Field Marshal. How do you view this renewed warmth?

A: Pakistan has a long history of using the Americans and manipulating the relationship. It has repeatedly managed to squeeze the US. It is not as though the Americans are unaware of how dangerously complex and devious Pakistan can be. There have always been determined Americans who understood the problem very well. Bruce Riedel, for example, advised several American presidents, including Bill Clinton and George W Bush, and he explained in detail why Pakistan should not be trusted. I quote an interesting anecdote in one of my books. Clinton was once asked what kept him awake at night. His answer was: “Pakistan.” So, the Americans know what they are dealing with. And yet they falter. Circumstances sometimes intervene.

As for Trump, he was shown the prospect of billions of dollars, and he bought it. And when it comes to things such as cryptocurrency, one wonders who in Pakistan has the money to buy it. It would have to be wealthy actors from countries such as Saudi Arabia or Qatar, or perhaps smugglers and drug dealers. But then Trump can do such things without shocking anyone.
